items.title: Exercise with UK, Canadian forces sharpens Kentucky Air Guard capabilities
items.author: Dale Greer
items.summary: Airmen from the Kentucky Air National Guard significantly enhanced their global capability in Scotland recently, working directly with NATO partners from the United Kingdom and Canada to execute dozens of multinational training events.
items.body:
Airmen from the Kentucky Air National Guard significantly enhanced their global capability here last month, working directly with NATO partners from the United Kingdom and Canada to execute dozens of multinational training events.

The Kentucky Guardsmen deployed four C-130J Super Hercules aircraft, 62,000 pounds of equipment and 60 personnel to Glasgow Prestwick Airport between Aug. 14 and 22, according to Lt. Col. Nick Reinke, mission commander and a C-130 pilot and assigned to the 165th Airlift Squadron.

While here, they conducted specialized fueling operations, low-level formation flying and rapid-reaction aircraft launches to maintain combat mission certifications, he said. The Airmen also completed maritime equipment and personnel airdrops, including two open-ocean rescue scenarios with a helicopter unit from the British Royal Navy.

“The deployment was designed to accomplish a large amount of C-130J continuation and tactical training while taking advantage of an unfamiliar overseas operating environment and opportunities to work directly with Allied partners,” Reinke said.

“While we can accomplish many of these individual training events in the United States, it is much harder to reproduce an unfamiliar environment. At home station, crews know the airspace, air traffic control procedures, airfields, support agencies and local practices. In Scotland, even something as routine as a proficiency circuit required crews to understand and coordinate with a different ATC system. Specialized fueling required coordination with host nation agencies, formation flying required United Kingdom low-level flying approval and integration with another nation’s C-130J, and the water rescue missions required coordination with us, a British helicopter unit and 16 Airmen from the Kentucky Air Guard’s 123rd Special Tactics Squadron.

“That forces crews to solve the kinds of interoperability, communication, planning and adaptation problems they encounter when operating globally. Worldwide capability is more than simply being able to fly across the Atlantic. It means arriving with the people and equipment needed to operate, understanding an unfamiliar airspace and support structure, integrating with Allied forces, adapting when weather or circumstances change the plan, and continuing to accomplish the mission.”

Reinke said the deployment also underscored the importance of relationships.

The Kentucky unit, based in Louisville, worked closely with civilian support agencies at Prestwick to complete specialized fueling operations, during which a C-130J was refueled while its engines were still running. This so-called “hot pit” method “validated Prestwick’s ability to support the technique and provided practical experience to host-nation fuel personnel,” Reinke said.

“That partnership leaves behind a more capable location for follow-on and Allied forces in the future, rather than the benefit ending when our deployment ended,” he noted.

One of the deployment’s key accomplishments was a five-ship formation flight, conducted with four Kentucky aircraft and one C-130J from the Royal Canadian Air Force.

“One of the interesting aspects was that the Canadian aircraft commander was actually a U.S. Marine Corps exchange pilot,” Reinke said. “That meant our mission planning and briefing had to reconcile U.S. Air Force, Royal Canadian Air Force and U.S. Marine Corps procedures and terminology to make sure everyone had the same understanding before execution. That is exactly the kind of interoperability that is difficult to simulate.”

The deployment’s other main focus was open-ocean rescue. The scenario required a C-130 crew to locate a stranded Airman floating in a life raft on the Atlantic Ocean, miles from shore. Loadmasters then airdropped an inflatable motorboat near the victim, and three Special Tactics Airmen used precision jumpmaster techniques to parachute into the ocean, deploy the boat and provide first aid. Once complete, they began coordination with the Royal Navy’s 814 Naval Air Squadron to execute helicopter hoist operations and extract the victim as the C-130 provided overwatch.

“The integration with the Royal Navy was one of the highlights of the exercise,” Reinke said. “It allowed our pararescue personnel and C-130J crews to integrate fixed-wing airdrop, maritime rescue, rotary-wing insertion/recovery and on-scene command and control with a NATO partner.”

A pararescue flight chief for the Special Tactics team described the operating environment in Scotland as “vastly different” from the locations they normally use for training in the United States.

“It’s a lot colder here, and the salt water is an unusual factor for us,” he said. “The Royal Navy also uses different geolocation methods, and they have different tactics and techniques than we typically employ.”

He noted that the Royal Navy’s helicopter, a Merlin Mk2, generates substantially more rotor wash than the UH-60 Black Hawks that the Kentuckians are used to.

“Those are the kinds of things you don’t anticipate, but we were able to work through them and figure out what worked best for their guys and for us,” the Airman said. “We had to be flexible on the spot to get the mission done.” Royal Navy Capt. James Hall said the exercise provided valuable opportunities for the Merlin Mk2 force to enhance capabilities outside its normal role in anti-submarine warfare.

“Exercises such as this, conducted alongside our United States Air Force partners, enable our crews to maintain and enhance critical search and rescue skills while strengthening the interoperability that underpins NATO’s collective security,” he said.

Lt. S. Cass, a flight commander for 814 Naval Air Squadron, agreed, adding that “we hope to continue working with our friends across the pond in the years to come.”

Reinke called the deployment an unqualified success, “not necessarily for any single event, but for how much readiness training we were able to layer into one exercise.”

“We were able to use legitimate flight training requirements to generate maximum value, ensuring worldwide readiness while working with our international partners. We also were able to build strong human relationships with the men and women of our partner nations, laying the kind of foundation that makes collation operations successful.”

items.title: Drowning in Data: New Report Says Space Force Needs Lasers Comms to Beat the Bottleneck
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The long-standing method for communicating data down from space via radio frequencies has the potential to create deadly data bottlenecks that could slow and stymie future operations, according to a new report from AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. The report makes the case for combining RF with optical communications technology, or laser comms, for a “hybrid” system. The post Drowning in Data: New Report Says Space Force Needs Lasers Comms to Beat the Bottleneck appeare
items.body:
The Space Force is preparing to launch hundreds of satellites with countless sensors into orbit over the next few years—sensors that will give commanders vast troves of data.

But the long-standing method for communicating data down from space via radio frequencies has the potential to create deadly data bottlenecks that could slow and stymie future operations, according to a new report.

The report, to be rolled out Oct. 1 by AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, makes the case for combining RF with optical communications technology, or laser comms, for a “hybrid” system.

Retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, now Mitchell’s senior resident fellow for space studies, authored the 37-page analysis and recommends that USSF get moving soon.

Her findings show that the military’s space-based sensors and communications systems are generating as much as 200 times more data than the force consumed two decades ago.

The ability to collect data, however, has not been matched yet by the ability to deliver it quickly to users, Reeves said.

The Space Force has made some moves to field laser comms, which advocates say is harder to disrupt and capable of transmitting more data faster. The Space Development Agency plans to field hundreds of data transport satellites with optical communications terminals in low-Earth orbit for its Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture.

In a Sept. 29 media briefing, Reeves called that effort “an important step towards … building a proliferated network designed to move data across space and ultimately to the warfighter. But that’s one piece of a much larger communications architecture.”

The first batch of operational data transport satellites is in orbit, and scores more are already under contract and being prepped for launch. The problem is that all of that data is being pushed through a legacy network never designed for that volume, according to Reeves’ report.

“I think the space layer is getting out ahead of us, and we’re going to have too much information to be able to manage effectively,” Reeves said. “We really need to earnestly move forward.”

Yet even as Reeves and others argue for the Space Force to develop laser comms even more, there has been pushback. In 2025, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported on a Government Accountability Office report that dinged the service for spending too much on the not-yet-ready-for-prime-time tech.

“Without demonstrating key laser communications technology capabilities, or [minimum viable products], SDA is risking not being able to leverage past experiences into the investments either under contract or planned for in the future,” GAO wrote. “These investments are substantial—nearly $35 billion.”

RF and Lasers

Radio frequency methods work by broadcasting RF down from space, which makes signals easy to detect, intercept, and jam with the right equipment and skills.

“The [laser] link is so much safer just because of that beam spread, that’s so tiny compared to what you’re getting with RF,” Reeves said in a Sept. 28 media briefing. “Whereas anything inside the footprint of RF, all you have to do to overcome is use power, and you are turning that off.”

As an example, she showed RF communications from space blanketing much of the United States East Coast, while a laser comms shot covered the equivalent to the size of Ellis Island, home of the Statue of Liberty.

“A much smaller footprint reduces spillover and the opportunity for detection, interception, or interference,” she said.

Laser comms can transport data 10 to 40 times faster using a beam nearly 1,000 times narrower. But that precision comes with reliability tradeoffs.

Satellites in low-Earth orbit travel at about 17,000 miles per hour. At that speed, the time window to find another satellite and blast a laser beam to it while keeping the link steady is small. Any physical movement, even small vibrations, can disrupt the signal.

Reeves doesn’t want to ditch RF. The report highlights the technology’s capabilities and its widespread use and applications. But it can’t be the only method, she said.

Moving Data Smarter

Additionally, the report identifies a need for on-platform edge processing to use AI tools and data filtering in space.

“Edge processing and artificial intelligence can help identify and prioritize what’s operationally relevant,” Reeves said.

That will avoid raw data eating up tons of bandwidth on the front end, she said.

The edge processing challenge is that most space assets currently still rely on ground station downlinks for complex command-and-control decisions and target processing, among other tasks. That’s largely due to thermal, power, and radiation thresholds on much space hardware.

In the near-term, USSF’s work building the Space Data Network aims to standardize optical inner satellite links and edge routing.

By using onboard sensor triage methods, USSF hopes that equipment can better process high-resolution imagery and other data on the space asset.

While the paper notes tech fixes such as laser comms and edge processing to move data around space and down to and back up from Earth, Reeves also advocates for reducing data flows and building self-healing, smart networks that reroute information to the best possible pathway to deliver relevant information to operational commanders in minutes, not hours.

“The goal isn’t simply to move every bit faster. It’s to move the right information towards the right user for the most effective available pathway,” Reeves said in the media briefing.

Building out a hybrid RF/laser space communications network isn’t an overnight affair. But Reeves argues an initial operational capability could be running within the next five years if Congress and DAF prioritize funding to mature the technology.

That, she said, is critical because the Chinese military isn’t ignoring this capability.

The Chinese government and People’s Liberation Army have two major satellite projects, both utilizing laser communications— the Guowang Constellation (National Network), and the Qianfan Constellation (Thousand Sails).

Guowang began launches in 2024 and currently has as many as 204 active satellites, with plans to deploy nearly 13,000. It uses standard broadband RF, high-resolution radar, and high-capacity laser cross links. The Chinese government views this network as an unjammable military communications backbone for the PLA.

Qianfan has 248 active satellites, Reeves said. It aims to contain 15,000 satellites by 2030. This network is the Chinese government’s testbed for optical terminals with high-speed laser nodes and has secondary military communication lines and maritime tracking assets.

For the U.S., optical communications are already in use among industry and some NASA satellites.

The agency has used the technology on its Orion spacecraft during the Artemis II mission, testing high-bandwidth video transmission from the distance of the Moon, or nearly 240,000 miles away.

The NASA Psyche spacecraft has conducted experiments with laser communications on deep-space laser links. And in 2021, the agency launched the Laser Communications Relay Demonstration and has conducted more than 2,600 experiments with its two ground stations.

The Space Force is also working on its Enterprise Space Terminal program, a $100 million prototyping initiative to build smaller, lighter laser comms terminals that use a standardized waveform.

Mitchell Report Recommendations

- Accelerate and Sustain Communications Modernization Through Stable Resourcing and Adaptive Acquisition.

- Operationalize Hybrid RF-Optical Architectures Across the Force

- Lead Interoperability and Standards Development for the Future Communications Ecosystem

items.body:
WINDSOR LOCKS, Conn. - On August 29 and 30, the New England Air Museum hosted its first annual WWII Weekend, a World War II reenactment that featured an Allied and Axis encampment, period vehicle demonstrations, as well as a historically themed hangar dance.

The event was organized by 43ID 169th Co. F, a World War II reenactment group that portrays and honors soldiers from the Connecticut Army National Guard’s 169th Infantry Regiment.

The 169th is one of the oldest continuously serving infantry regiments in the United States, tracing its lineage back to 1637. During World War II, the regiment served in the Pacific Theater of Operations, and participated in the New Georgia, Northern Solomons and Luzon campaigns. Today, the regiment serves as part of the Regional Training Institute based at Camp Nett in Niantic. Their mission is to provide national coordinating authority, quality assurance, and scheduling and accreditation assistance for functionally aligned ARNG elements within the Army School System.

43ID 169th Co. F was formed in 2020 by Tolland native, Douglas Crawford. Crawford’s father, Charles, was an infantryman assigned to Fox Company, 2nd Battalion, 169th Infantry Regiment, during World War II. He enlisted in 1939, was federalized with the rest of the 43rd Infantry Division in 1941 and, after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, destined for the Pacific. His unit would depart San Francisco on September 30, 1942, and spend 22 days out at sea before arriving in Auckland, New Zealand. Charles and the regiment engaged in an intense training regimen here as well as in New Caledonia. Following some time on Guadalcanal and Pavuvu, Charles and the 169th would participate in Operation Toenails, the drive on Munda Point to capture a strategic Japanese airfield.

“He remembered vividly [that] the Japanese [used] sleep deprivation as one of their tactics against American soldiers, keeping them up all night for days on end,” explained Douglas. “Sleeping in a foxhole back to back with your buddy. He always said how they would never strap their helmet’s [chinstrap] because the Japanese would sneak into your foxhole and pull you out by your helmet. If you had your chinstrap on, it was easy to pull you out.”

Charles would survive the war, eventually being evacuated back to the United States in 1944 for combat neurosis, an acute, and often debilitating, psychological reaction that stems directly from war trauma. Combat neurosis, and other combat related stresses, affected over 15% of 43rd Infantry Division soldiers during Operation Toenails, the highest rate of neuropsychiatric casualties for any division during one singular operation throughout the war. After the war, he would have 13 children, Douglas being his last.

Eventually, Douglas had a son of his own, Mason. As Mason grew older, he expressed an interest in history and began reenacting with his father. Together, the pair reenacted soldiers from the 5th Connecticut Regiment during the Revolutionary War. However, after portraying this era of history for a decade, Mason began expressing more interest in his grandfather’s wartime service.

“I was always interested in World War II; we watched The Pacific and we watched Band of Brothers, and I knew both my grandfathers had fought [in the war],” explained Mason. “My mom’s father was on the USS New Jersey from ‘41 to ‘45, and my dad’s father was in from ‘39 to [‘44]. We started off doing Rev War because we didn’t know that there were too many World War II reenactment groups around, and not too many that were super interesting. I didn’t have that personal attachment to it. After, like, 10 years, I started getting really burnt out of Rev War and I really wanted to get into World War II. Me and [Douglas] sat down, and we had another couple guys who wanted to do World War II as well, we all kind of sat down and collaborated and we’re thinking about it, what should we do? Let’s start our own unit.”

Despite the pair now having a rich personal history to bond over, and a newly established reenactment group as the outlet for this passion, there still wasn’t any arena to expand this experience. In the reenacting world, there are two major types of events, living histories, and tacticals. Living histories are events put on for the public, allowing spectators to get a glimpse of what life was like during a particular era or among a certain group. Tacticals are immersive simulated combat events, normally conducted privately between multiple reenactment groups who will recreate a battle between opposing forces. Connecticut largely offered neither of these styles of events for those interested in World War II, as the bulk of the local reenactment community is largely focused on the state’s rich Revolutionary War and Civil War history.

To remedy this, Douglas worked with Tianna Darling, the New England Air Museum’s operations and program director, to establish an event.

“I was on Facebook and I saw a post from the New England Air Museum, and they posted something to do with World War II and I wrote in the comments, we would love to do an event there, you know ‘hey, what about doing a World War II reenactment’, and not five minutes later I got a response from Tianna Darling, here at the museum, she was the new operations manager,” explained Douglas. “She's like, ‘oh my God, we were just having a meeting last night and I was mentioning we should do something like that’. So, it’s like, almost fate that night they were having that meeting. The next day they make that post. There I am. Every idea, every plan I submitted to her, she was like, ‘yes, let’s do it. Let’s do it.’”

Crawford and Tianna communicated back and forth for over a year via emails and zoom meetings. After working together for a smaller event as a test run, the pair went forward and green lit having a World War II weekend.

“We worked with them in a smaller capacity, and then finally we said, ‘yeah, let’s do it, let’s do something larger',” explained Tianna. “He brought to our attention that there is not a lot of reenactment of this scale in this area in Connecticut. There’s some up in Massachusetts with the Collings Foundation, and then there’s some smaller scale stuff, but there was kinda a need for that, and it really works with our mission. We work to preserve and educate on aerospace history, specifically in the New England region as well as around the country, so it fit really well with our mission and it was wonderful that they were able to reach out to us.”

For reenactors, events like these are very special as it gives them the opportunity to interact with and educate the public on the trials and sacrifices faced by service members during World War II. Most spend countless hours referencing historical reporting, analyzing period photographs, reading memoirs and watching veteran interviews related to the unit they are portraying. Additionally, they dedicate much time, and money, in acquiring period uniforms, equipment, and weaponry, or accurate reproductions. Likewise, events like these bring the community together, as it gives veterans, their relatives, and friends, the opportunity to connect, share their experiences, and keep their memory alive.

“I had more people come up that had relatives that were in the 169th, that wanted to bring me their books, their info. This one lady had a complete photo album of her father, who actually served in I Company, my father was in F Company, they were in the same book. She had pictures I had never seen of the regiment,” explained Douglas. “Obviously this was something she put together, a labor of love for her father, but who really is she going to show it to? Yeah, she showed it to her family, but she doesn’t really get to show it to anybody else. Here we are, the 169th, bring it in here and show it to us, and I could see it in her eyes, the happiness that she could share that.”

In addition to the F. Co, 169th, over 200 reenactors dressed in authentic military uniforms were present throughout the encampment representing and recounting their unit’s histories and achievements, including the Capital Wing of the Airmen’s Preservation Society, portraying the United States Army Air Forces, Geronimo Foundation, Inc., portraying paratroopers from the 501st Parachute Infantry Battalion; Fox Company, 2nd Battalion, 5th Marine Regiment, Reenacted; and the New England Red Devils, 7th Parachute Bn Living History Association and 1st Canadian Parachute Battalion Preservation Association, representing the British Commonwealth, among others. An impressive armada of privately owned historic vehicles bolstered the museum’s static displays for the event, including jeeps, an M5 light tank, an M8 light armored car, and a Sturmgeschütz III assault gun. To make the event even more spectacular, nine WWII veterans including Technician 4th Grade Caster Salemi, 251st Field Artillery Battalion, and U.S. Marine Corps veteran Ted Marolda, 1st Marine Division, attended the event, giving attendees an unforgettable, and increasingly rare, opportunity to hear first hand accounts of what it was like to serve during the war.

“It’s such a different way to experience history because it’s something you’ll never get from a textbook, or even, you know, watching a movie,” said Tianna. “You’re able to talk with these people who are so invested in historical accuracy. They know in and out what they are portraying. Even if you’re someone who doesn’t think they’re interested in history or aviation, you’re able to learn something new and have a great time doing it. One of the groups we had here, we had them back a couple of times, they portrayed air raid precaution wardens in Britain during the war, and we were absolutely fascinated. They were showing us all of the different sirens they had, fire suppression systems, and all this stuff. They had the materials right there. They could talk to it, so even as staff, we were learning new things as we went. I think it is just a really unique way to experience history.”

The general public seemed to agree as they descended on the museum in droves. 984 tickets were sold on Saturday, not including the 200 tickets sold exclusively for the hangar dance later that night. Sunday, saw similar attendance rates, even with the weather being cloudy with scattered bursts of light rain throughout the afternoon.

“It was fantastic,” explained Tianna. “We are so thrilled with how the event turned out. It is, anecdotally, our largest public weekend event in recent memory. That’s for sure. We had 1,700 people come through our doors between Saturday, Sunday and our hangar dance on Saturday evening. People came from all over…it was just a really cool experience to see all these people just so interested in coming and experiencing the museum, learning about this history. It went amazing, and we’ll definitely be doing it again next year for sure.”

items.title: Energizing the Technology of Tomorrow
items.author: Daniel Linehan
items.summary: Joint Interagency Field Experimentation (JIFX) events continue to advance and accelerate the development of new technologies that are vital across the joint force for readiness and battlefield advantage in contested environments.
items.body:
Joint Interagency Field Experimentation ( JIFX ) events continue to advance and accelerate the development of new technologies that are vital across the joint force for readiness and battlefield advantage in contested environments.

Autonomous swarming, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), uncrewed drones by land, sea, and air, counter-drone detection , high-energy laser weapon systems , GPS denied navigation, C5ISR (command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance) systems, advanced energy systems , and expeditionary additive manufacturing are just some of the wide-ranging technologies that have undergone experimentation and development at JIFX.

During a week of experimentation held in August 2026, nearly 200 uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) sorties executed experimental flight tests throughout the vast airspace accessible through JIFX . This brings the tally up to 635 sorties flown during the past year at the Naval Postgraduate School’s (NPS) quarterly JIFX events, held in southern Monterey County at the California National Guard’s Camp Roberts.

The sorties pushed the boundaries of new UAV designs and upgrades to existing UAV hardware, software, controls, and operations. Though the aim for each sortie differed, one immediate factor underscored each experiment — how energy and innovation drive advantage in the future.

Drone Dominance Fueled by JIFX

ModalAI, Firestorm (watch slow motion https://youtu.be/upa74ykT_iY), and Greensight (watch https://youtu.be/OF2LTJ4PYMM) participated in the U.S. Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program (DDP) competition, set to wrap up in 2027. Firestorm and Greensight are frequent JIFX attendees. And ModalAI, which attended JIFX twice, made it into the final DDP selection and is still in the running. So far, it has shipped over 2,000 drones to DDP.

Back at JIFX, a small fleet of ModalAI quadcopters, operated by Gambit Defense, also made an appearance. The Gambit test flights hit the radar of JIFX director and NPS faculty member Michael Richardson.

“The experiments with autonomous swarming activity by Gambit have been very powerful,” said Richardson, who is also a retired U.S. Army colonel and former special operations officer. “Gambit is a great example of the many companies that come to JIFX and show incredible promise, particularly with respect to advancing the drone warfare doctrine of Pacific Command.”

Gambit experimented with its AI/ML mesh network system under contested electronic warfare conditions. It flew dozens of sorties for autonomous target detection, follow, patrol, and swarm missions. When jammed, its drones automatically maintained communication.

Like Gambit, Rhoman Aerospace is a frequent participant at JIFX providing software solutions for different drone platforms. During a separate field experimentation effort, it provided a system for GPS-denied navigation over open water to NPS researchers and Naval Special Warfare operators.

Had it not been for experiments by Rhoman at previous JIFX iterations, this collaboration with NPS would not have happened.

“From JIFX to JIFX, we see industry make iterative development as we poke and push them in different directions,” Richardson emphasized. “JIFX is shaping change. It facilitates more effective connections between what emerging technologies can offer and the pressing needs of national security and defense.”

Innovations in Operational Energy

Reliant on batteries and liquid fuels, participants mobilized in hangars, on the tarmac, and along the flightline of Camp Roberts’ McMillan Airfield. From rows of workstations inside the Technical Operations Center, they also ran C5ISR experiments.

On a remote hill further across the base at the Combined Arms Collective Training Facility (CACTF), other experimenters interfaced systems with human operators to investigate urban structures from the air and ground. And, in between, GArmor’s experimental armored crew transport roved the surrounding terrain.

As UAVs buzzed above, new counter-UAV sensor technology scanned the sky to spot them with radiofrequency, passive radar, acoustic, and other forms of drone detection. These, too, needed reliable energy sources.

Optimizing the energy used by these technologies, through testing at JIFX, directly improves their application and longevity in operational environments.

“We see a lot of value in JIFX because energy is part of every technology, whether it requires energy, produces energy, or just absorbs energy,” said Michael Davis, associate chair of NPS’ Energy Academic Group and, like Richardson, a retired U.S. Army colonel and former special operations officer.

The Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment’s Operational Energy-Innovation (OE-I) Directorate recently began providing support to JIFX. Davis is tasked with scoping out technological trends at JIFX and determining how these trends could potentially impact tomorrow’s battlefield.

“JIFX expedites technology transition. It helps technologies quickly become operational. With energy technologies, this can be challenging across the landscape of the joint force,” said Davis. Of much interest to him were the bourgeoning technologies of Chargebotic and Haylon Technologies.

Chargebotic came to experiment at JIFX with its energy harvesting system. It used a UAV, modified with additive manufactured components printed on the spot, to clamp a tether onto a powerline to parasitically extract energy, extending its operational utility. After flight tests that dialed in the UAV’s altered performance characteristics, Chargebotic successfully attached to a live powerline suspended on a test rig and drew electricity from it.

This source of parasitic energy was just the kind of emerging energy trend Davis keeps an eye out for. Similarly, at JIFX in February 2026, Davis applauded Reach Power’s use of radio frequency waves to wirelessly beam energy that recharged the battery of a hovering UAV, increasing its station time by nearly ten-fold.

Haylon took a different approach to energy provision. Its multiple battery chemistry switching system allowed a device, such as a UAV, to receive uninterrupted energy from more than one type of battery. Switching depends on the device’s current performance requirements and the various strengths and optimal uses for different battery sources.

In the case of a UAV, which requires a large amount of energy for a short time during takeoff, it is powered by a battery type that can provide a boost of energy up front. But these types of batteries are quickly depleted.

Therefore, Haylon’s system would switch the battery type after takeoff. During the flight phase, the UAV would then be powered by a battery that cannot deliver high energy but instead provides a steady stream of energy over a prolonged duration. By mixing the best qualities of two different batteries, the UAV maximizes its energy efficiently, extending its operational range.

“We also want to make sure that we're not adding to the logistical burden as we build new technologies, especially facing future challenges like constrained logistics and contested environments,” added Davis. “So, by helping technologists understand this from early in their development and experimentation, we can help them avoid later slowdowns or complications as they get to higher transition readiness levels.”

JIFX by Land to BOMA by Sea

U.S. Navy Lt. Cmdr. Max Leutermann, an NPS and Special Operations Command (SOCOM) researcher, continued experimenting on a compact and mobile counter-drone system for boats used by special operations forces. As NPS students in 2025, Leutermann and Swedish Armed Forces Maj. Patrik Liljegard rapidly developed the system from scratch and used JIFX to field test an early-stage prototype that they mounted in a pickup truck’s bed.

“NATO required us to create a system that was passive so that operators who were on a small boat wouldn’t give off any sort of detectable signatures or emissions,” said Leutermann.

“While companies and other NPS students at JIFX flew their drones all around, we tried to detect them,” he continued. “Different types of drones at different altitudes, distances, directions, angles of attack. Our second goal at JIFX was processing what we detected and representing it on the navigation display.”

Building upon JIFX, they also successfully demonstrated the operation of their prototype aboard a proper boat at the Bold Machina (BOMA) 2025 exercise in the Netherlands, which was run by NATO Allied Special Operations Forces Command (SOFCOM).

The results were so promising that Leutermann and Liljegard reteamed months after having graduating from NPS, with SOCOM, NATO SOFCOM, and the Swedish Armed Forces providing support and funding for the continued development of the system.

At the latest JIFX, Leutermann and three Swedish programmers experimented on a much-refined version of their counter-drone system in preparation for NATO’s next BOMA exercise, held in September 2026 in Portugal.

In addition to collaborations with Latent AI (AI dataset generation), Haylon (dual battery chemistry), and Bellum Systems (passive radar), Leutermann’s counter-drone system was powered by Chargebotic using an expeditionary battery from Chariot Defense .

Last year at JIFX, Chariot had experimented with mobile, low-signature, and high energy battery development and powered Aurelius’ laser weapon system for drone defense and Firestorm’s expeditionary additive manufacturing station for drone building.

During the September BOMA — weeks after JIFX in August — Leutermann reported that he was making excellent progress on the Operational Data Integration Node (ODIN) of the c-UAV system. ODIN is an AI-driven, sensor fusion engine that collects and centralizes all data from the various sensor platforms connected to the system.

“BOMA showed that the core ODIN architecture works in the field,” said Leutermann from Portugal. “We demonstrated passive RF cueing, autonomous visual search and tracking — including an RF-dark drone with no operator interaction — and ingested RADAR data into ODIN.”

An Advanced Technology Proving Ground Like No Other

What separates JIFX from field exercises and demonstrations focused on developing defense science and technology is that JIFX focuses on experimental campaigns — not the sales and marketing campaigns often seen at other venues. Participants conduct experiments with work-in-progress technology. They do not demonstrate polished products like at a tradeshow.

Over 30 experimental campaigns were successfully completed at the August JIFX by different organizations, which also led to many collaborative experiments between them.

Three focus areas emerged from the technology of these campaigns:

AI-enabled decision advantage - experiments aimed at helping operators rapidly transform large volumes of data into actionable information.

Autonomous systems in contested environments - experiments sought to improve the resilience and effectiveness of autonomous systems operating in denied, degraded, and contested conditions.

Expeditionary sustainment and edge operations - experiments addressed the challenges of sustaining distributed forces in austere environments.

As a proving ground, JIFX affords a safe and secure environment with an infrastructure that allows participants to operate under real-world conditions and push their technology to the limits — and often beyond. Stakeholders from across the joint force with operational knowledge and experience provide the experimenters with insights into the actual needs of those in the field.

With the sprawling Camp Roberts as its backdrop, JIFX most recently hosted 269 participants from industry, defense, and academia organizations. As with past events, mid-career officers came to observe . They were students from across the service branches and international commands who are studying at NPS.

Most of these students were fresh from military deployments and had highly relevant experience related to the technologies undergoing experimentation at JIFX. They knew what worked well for them, what didn’t work, and the operational and technological gaps that still needed to be filled. This gave them valuable perspectives into practical applications and operational uses, which they readily shared with the experimenters.

The experimenters found the knowledge the students shared had helpful impacts on the development of their technologies. This two-way street exposed the students to innovation and emerging technologies at stages of development much earlier than they would have encountered operationally during their regular duties.

U.S. Army Capt. Evan Prince, a Defense Analysis student who’s looking to add Information Sciences as a second major, was among the group of 60 students in attendance.

“I was really excited when I saw Watchtower, which is an AI-enabled system that basically ingests intelligence to create most likely and most dangerous courses of action taken by a would-be adversary,” he said. “They're working on a solution that can fill a gap that I’m looking at.” Developed by Panoptica Technologies, Watchtower helps generate and expedite threat assessments for military intelligence analysts.

“The initial reason why they popped out to me was because of my thesis,” Prince added. “Watchtower has great potential, and if its scope is able to expand a bit to cover the actual gap I've seen operationally, then I think it's something that can support our force very well.”

Prince is also a Meyer Scholar , an NPS program exposing students to a wide range of technologies operationally relevant to the modern battlespace. He found the program prepared him for an even more meaningful engagement with Panoptica at JIFX.

“It's what equipped me for the conversation I had about Watchtower,” he said.

His experience at JIFX highlights how bringing students and experimenters together can create meaningful connections between emerging technologies and operational challenges.

Defense Technology Pipeline and Range of the Future

JIFX does not only foster technology, but it also evolves with it. Exemplifying this was the experimental Defense Innovation Network Assistant (DINA) TAK (Tactical Assault Kit), which integrated data from Gambit, MicroVision, Insignito Solutions, Bellum Systems, and others into a sensor fused, shared operational data environment.

Developed in collaboration between Naval Surface Warfare Center (NSWC) Corona, California Baptist University, NPS, Standard TLM, and other partners, DINA TAK moves JIFX closer into the realm of live-virtual-constructive (LVC) experimentation ranges.

DINA TAK, a government AI tool, is designed to enable future integration and JIFX expansion to a true LVC experimentation range. DINA TAC benefits from the wide range of technologies that help expand and refine the tool, which in turn increases JIFX's ability to support ad hoc integration and coordination among participants.

Troy Clarke, the Inland Empire Tech Bridge director at NSWC Corona, briefed government stakeholders at JIFX about DINA TAK and its connection to LVC experimentation ranges.

“We introduce new technology into the ranges that we could then incorporate into the actual tactical training ranges,” Clarke said.

But the initial stage of development simply had experimenters inputting their data from telemetry, sensor networks, and other ISR (intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance) sources with ATAK (Android tactical assault kit) devices. DINA TAK then used AI-enabled data aggregation to support visualization, real-time tracking, after-action reconstruction, and more.

Once fully established, the “Range of the Future” could become a resource for others from across industry to also conduct experimentation. And for stakeholders scouting technology, DINA TAK has the potential to provide up-to-date and in-depth assessments backed by proven supporting data.

“JIFX is a very unique and special environment where you can bring early-stage technology and integrate with other innovators who are trying to figure out their niche and how they're going to get their technology across the joint force,” said Jason Hay, director of technology at BryceTech.

Hay attended JIFX as contract support to stakeholders, where he soaked in and evaluated DINA TAK and the other technologies. By gaining this understanding, he now looks to leverage JIFX for accelerating technologies.

The rapid pace of experimentation throughout the vast land, sea, and air laboratory and the extensive collaboration between participants impressed him, and he sees JIFX as a vital pipeline for defense science and technology.

“Just like you have to stockpile munitions, you have to stockpile innovation,” Hay said. “A supply of intelligence, knowledge, and data is necessary for the development of future technologies. If you don't have people exploring the early stages of technology, then the supply will dry up. The good news is that JIFX is here to keep the experiments running and on course.”

NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters and leaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

items.title: Renovated MOTCO Resident Office Gives USACE Team a Home Built for Collaboration
items.author: Grant Okubo
items.summary: After a seven-month renovation, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District has reopened its resident office at Military Ocean Terminal Concord in a fully remodeled Building 262, giving staff a permanent, unified home for the first time since the resident office was established over a decade ago. The renovation, part of a project officially named the MOTCO Resident Office Remodel, focused on Building 262 and ran from January to July 2026. Crews refinished most of the building's interior
items.body:
After a seven-month renovation, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District has reopened its resident office at Military Ocean Terminal Concord in a fully remodeled Building 262, giving staff a permanent, unified home for the first time since the resident office was established over a decade ago.

The renovation, part of a project officially named the MOTCO Resident Office Remodel, focused on Building 262 and ran from January to July 2026. Crews refinished most of the building's interior walls, removed hazardous materials, installed new entry doors and signage, and built an entrance with a compliant accessible path to the parking area.

The building has a long history at MOTCO. Built in the mid-20th century, it has served multiple functions over the decades. Its most recent job before the remodel was serving as headquarters for the installation's police department, a role it held into the mid-2000s.

"The facility needed a complete rehabilitation," said Emmanuel Torres Reyes, supervisory architect and resident engineer for the MOTCO Resident Office. Police had used it as a tactical training ground, and it carried many of the same issues as the office's old temporary building. Access was limited. Some walls held mold and other hazardous materials. And the mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems weren't built to support the number of staff USACE planned to house there. It even lacked a safe means to access the building.

According to Torres Reyes, the renovation allows the MOTCO mission to operate efficiently and house all required disciplines under one roof.

"Our main designers were sitting at the Directorate of Public Works building, the safety and unexploded ordnance staff had to work out of their cars or travel back and forth between J Street and MOTCO," he said. "Now the office is truly collaborative and issues that come up are addressed much quicker."

The design team included spaces meant to encourage exactly that kind of collaboration: a reading lounge, a plan review area, and a conference room for project delivery team meetings and both remote and in-person training. Cubicles throughout the office use glass panels instead of solid walls, a deliberate move away from the darker layouts common in older government buildings.

One detail Torres Reyes said doesn't come through in photos is the way the building welcomes people, from the approach to the entrance itself. Multiple changes in scale along the way are meant to make every arrival feel like coming to a real workplace. Lighting along the walkway shifts in stages, from overhead parking lights to shorter poles at the curb to bollards that illuminate sequentially as staff walk toward the entrance. The lobby ceiling runs nearly double height before stepping down as it opens into the office space.

"That is something not obvious in pictures but perceived in space," Torres Reyes said.

The main goal is to offer MOTCO employees a safe place to effectively and efficiently execute the mission.

“Staff can now pull together for plan readings, research code in the lounge, or work through a problem with contractors and stakeholders without leaving the building,” he said.

Even small additions, such as filtered water, a coffee station, a team wall and USACE signage throughout the building made a big impression on morale once the project wrapped.

"The importance and impact of branding and workplace design is often neglected. It plays a crucial role in employee satisfaction and productivity by instilling a sense of pride and ownership," he said.

items.title: NAVFAC Northwest awards record-breaking $9 billion multiple award construction contract
items.author: Amanda Surmeier
items.summary: In a historic achievement for naval infrastructure delivery, Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Northwest awarded a $9 billion indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity, multiple-award construction contract (MACC) Sept. 30. Marking the largest single procurement action in NAVFAC Northwest history, the command selected 15 industry-leading construction partners for the award just before the close of the fiscal year – a testament to months of rigorous planning, complex market resea
items.body:
In a historic achievement for naval infrastructure delivery, Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Northwest awarded a $9 billion indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity, multiple-award construction contract (MACC) Sept. 30.

Marking the largest single procurement action in NAVFAC Northwest history, the command selected 15 industry-leading construction partners for the award just before the close of the fiscal year – a testament to months of rigorous planning, complex market research, and exhaustive coordination across the enterprise.

Behind the Scenes: Acquisition Excellence Executing an acquisition vehicle valued at $9 billion requires an extraordinary level of precision, endurance, and technical acumen. Crossing the finish line on Sept. 30 culminated months of long hours, negotiations, and intense dedication by NAVFAC Northwest’s acquisition and contracting professionals.

The contracting team spearheaded the development of intricate source-selection criteria, navigated multi-agency regulatory compliances, and evaluated over 20 comprehensive proposals to assemble this historic vehicle.

"This is not just a standard award – it is a generational milestone that our contracting and acquisition workforce achieved through relentless commitment to the Navy mission," said NAVFAC Northwest Commanding Officer Capt. Bob Stiles. "To bring a contract of this scale and technical complexity across the finish line on the final day of the fiscal year is nothing short of extraordinary. Their tenacity gives us the tools to ensure our shore installations will maintain the operational readiness the Fleet requires for years to come."

Building for the Future: Broad Scope, Lasting Impact The contract structure includes a one-year base period, two two-year options, and one three-year option period, spanning up to 96 months through September 2034. While the vehicle encompasses work across the region, the vast majority will directly revitalize and modernize military installations throughout Washington State. The contracting team engineered this vehicle as a versatile, rapid-response delivery option that actively supports virtually every facet of shore infrastructure, including:

Mission-Critical & Specialized Facilities: Advanced aviation hangars, Special Access Program Facilities, Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities, industrial fabrication plants, and maintenance hubs.

Energy, Grid & Utility Resilience: High-voltage substations, electrical distribution modernization, power and communication corridors, and critical storm-water/culvert infrastructure.

Operational & Civil Infrastructure: Airfield pavement overhauls, arterial roadway and bridge reconstruction, tactical training ranges, and waterfront production facilities.

Quality of Life & Force Support: State-of-the-art medical and dental clinics, modernized personnel barracks and lodging, administrative centers, and recreational facilities.

By establishing this robust 15-firm contractor pool, NAVFAC Northwest secures the delivery speed and competitive capacity needed to execute urgent task orders quickly, delivering top-tier engineering and construction solutions to the Fleet.

For more information on this contract, please contact the NAVFAC Northwest Public Affairs Office at mailto:navfacnwpao@us.navy.mil.

– USN –

Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command is the naval shore facilities, base operating support, and expeditionary engineering systems command that delivers life-cycle technical and acquisition solutions aligned to the fleet and Marine Corps priorities. Follow us at http://www.facebook.com/navfacnorthwest and http://www.linkedin.com/showcase/navfacnorthwest

items.title: Idaho Army National Guard conducts two search and rescues in back-to-back days
items.author: MAJ Robert Taylor
items.summary: The Idaho Army National Guard conducted two successful search and rescue missions last week after conducting three such missions the week before.
items.body: The Idaho Army National Guard conducted two successful search and rescue missions last week after conducting three such missions the week before. On Sept. 23, a UH-60M Black Hawk crew assisted with the search and rescue of a lost individual in Idaho County. On the following day, a different crew assisted with the rescue of a hiker in the Owyhee Mountains. “Our Soldiers train for missions all over the world, but there's no more immediate way to see the value of that training than when they're called upon to help an Idahoan in trouble,” said Brig. Gen. Eric Orcutt, commander of the Idaho Army National Guard. “These crews bring an incredible level of skill and professionalism to some of the most difficult environments in our state, and they continue to demonstrate why the Idaho National Guard is such an important part of Idaho's emergency-response capability.” Flight crews assisted Tuesday and Wednesday with the search for a lost individual near Riggins in the vicinity of Kelly Mountain who had last been seen since Sunday. Idaho County officials and volunteers located the man Wednesday in the Looking Glass Creek drainage west of Kelly Mountain and notified the Idaho Army National Guard’s flight operations desk that the man had been found. However, due to limited communication in the remote mountainous area, the flight crew was unaware he had been located and continued their search. Chief Warrant Officer 3 Arlin Knight, the mission’s pilot in command, said he could see a search party volunteer waving down the crew in a thick wooded area. Knight said the area looked too dense to land a helicopter and that a hoist helicopter would be needed to conduct the rescue. The Black Hawk was not equipped with a hoist or other rescue equipment because the crew's mission was to search as large an area as possible. Leaving the additional equipment behind reduced the aircraft's weight and gave the crew more time to remain on station. Knight said the crew decided to make a pass over the sight in an attempt to find somewhere to land. The crew attempted to land in a confined area close to the patient, but was only able to get one wheel on the ground due to the slope and did not feel it was a safe landing space. The crew identified a second landing place, which required close coordination between the helicopter’s two crew chiefs and the pilots. “Landing in a place like that, it all depends on the crew chiefs to communicate to the pilot so that you’re clear of the trees,” said Knight. “You have to come down just right in a confined area.” After landing, Knight said the crew was running short on time due to fuel and that the two crew chiefs, Staff Sgt. Dakota Miller and Sgt. Robert Watkins, traversed approximately 500 meters to reach the patient and those who found him. Miller said that when they reached the patient, he was loaded on a soft litter. Miller told a deputy on scene that they could transport the man if they could get him to the helicopter. Miller, Watkins, the deputy, and three volunteers then carried the man to the helicopter using a two-foot wide game trial over logs and rocks and down and back up a ravine to reach the Black Hawk. “We really thought there was no way to get in there without a hoist, but we found a way in,” said Knight. “The real shout out goes to Miller and Watkin, who conducted three confined landing zones after flying for six hours and then they went and got this guy and carried him back over to the helicopter in all their flight gear.” The Black Hawk crew then transported the man to the 394 Road, which required a third confined landing. The patient was reunited with his family and transported to the McCall Hospital for civilian care. “We had already made the decision we weren’t going to be able to get to him,” said Miller. “The entire time we were landing the helicopter, we were thinking anything we do from here was icing on the cake. It was really cool to go further than we thought we could.” The Idaho County Sherriff’s Office, the Idaho Civil Air Patrol and the Idaho county Search and Rescue K9 unit assisted with the search. The next day, Sept. 24, a separate crew assisted the Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office, the Grand View Fire Department and the Idaho Mountain Search and Rescue Unit with the rescue of a 21-year-old male who was stranded clinging to a cliff several hundred feet above the ground in Purjue Canyon near Grand View. He was unable to climb up or down and utilized voice-to-text to contact his family and to call 911. The Idaho Army National Guard flight crew flew members of the Idaho Mountain Search and Rescue Unit technical rescue team to the top of the cliff. The team built a two-tension rope system at the top of the cliff using a rock as an anchor and lowered a rescuer to the man utilizing an “unsupported pick-off” technique. While the man clung to the rock face, the rescuer fitted him with a harness and both were then lowered to the ground. The man was not injured. The search and rescue missions were the 12th and 13th successful missions for the Idaho Army National Guard in 2026. The Idaho Army National Guard also conducted three successful rescue missions between Sept. 16-20.

items.title: Creech retires after four decades of service to Illinois National Guard
items.author: Zachary Zimerman
items.summary: After four decades of service that began as an enlisted Infantry Soldier and culminated with his service as the United States Property and Fiscal Officer for Illinois, Col. Brian S. Creech retired from the Illinois Army National Guard during a ceremony Sept. 18 at the Illinois Military Academy at Camp Lincoln.
items.body: After four decades of service that began as an enlisted Infantry Soldier and culminated with his service as the United States Property and Fiscal Officer for Illinois, Col. Brian S. Creech retired from the Illinois Army National Guard during a ceremony Sept. 18 at the Illinois Military Academy at Camp Lincoln. “I gave the Army everything I had, and it gave me back more than I expected,” Creech said. “He understood the tactical realities of supporting Soldiers in the field and the strategic responsibilities of managing resources,” said Brig. Gen. Ronnie Barnes, National Guard Bureau Comptroller. Brig. Gen. Barnes presided over the ceremony, which brought together family, friends, fellow service members, Illinois National Guard leaders, and multiple United States Property and Fiscal Officers from other states to recognize Creech's 40 years of military service. The United States Property and Fiscal Officer (USPFO) is a federally appointed officer who serves as the single Title 10 National Guard officer through which all federal resources flow to a state or territory’s National Guard. Barnes said that those in the USPFO community could always call Creech when they had a difficult problem. “His responses would always be thoughtful, honest, and grounded in experience,” Barnes said. “And they would always be straightforward.” Creech thanked several leaders who mentored and developed him, and all the subordinates who accomplished so much under his direction, but he especially thanked his family. “Every time the Army asked something of me, it asked something of you too,” he told his spouse, Stephanie. Creech began his military career in August 1986 as an enlisted Soldier with Company A, 1st Battalion, 123rd Infantry Regiment. During his enlisted service, he served as a rifleman and squad leader before receiving his commission as an Infantry second lieutenant in September 1996. His career included assignments in Infantry, Logistics, Financial Management, Human Resources and command positions throughout the Illinois National Guard. Creech served as a platoon leader and commander with the 3637th Maintenance Company and later held staff positions with the 232nd Combat Sustainment Support Battalion. In 2003, he deployed to Iraq with the 232nd CSSB in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom II. Just prior to being activated for Iraq, he “confidently” told his pregnant spouse, Stephanie, that “the National Guard never deploys.” He returned from Iraq on their son Bryson’s first birthday. “I learned never to make a promise on behalf of the U.S. Army,” he said. Following his deployment, Creech transferred to Joint Force Headquarters, Illinois, where he served as a logistics plans officer, budget officer, commander and financial manager. In May 2010, he began a Title 10 assignment with the National Guard Bureau as a program analyst for the Army National Guard Recruiting Division. While working as a program analyst for the Army National Guard Recruiting Division he provided professional, and characteristically straightforward ethical advice on several highly scrutinized programs including marketing contracts with NASCAR and World Wrestling Entertainment and the Guard Recruitment Assistance Program. He returned to Illinois in October 2010 and assumed duties as the USPFO supervisory logistics management specialist. From October 2013 through October 2016, he commanded the 405th Brigade Support Battalion. Creech subsequently returned to Joint Force Headquarters, where he served as the Human Resources Officer and deputy USPFO before assuming the position of USPFO for Illinois in September 2021. As USPFO, Creech oversaw critical personnel, financial and logistical functions supporting the Illinois National Guard. His service in the position included supporting multiple training and domestic operations while contributing to readiness across the organization. During the retirement ceremony, Creech was presented with the Legion of Merit for exceptionally meritorious service as the USPFO for Illinois. The award recognized his leadership and technical expertise and his contributions to personnel, finance and logistics readiness. Creech was also presented with his retirement certificate. His wife, Stephanie, received a spouse's certificate recognizing her support and dedication throughout his military career. A commitment to professional development accompanied Creech's military service. He earned a bachelor's degree in economics from the University of Illinois Springfield and graduated from the United States Army War College in 2018 with a master's degree in strategic studies. His military awards and decorations include the Legion of Merit, Bronze Star Medal, Meritorious Service Medal, Army Commendation Medal, Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal, Army Achievement Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Humanitarian Service Medal, Joint Meritorious Unit Award, Meritorious Unit Commendation, Combat Action Badge and Iraq Campaign Medal with campaign star, along with additional federal and state awards. Throughout the ceremony, Creech's family was recognized as an integral part of his military journey. He and Stephanie have been married for more than 24 years and have four sons, Zach, Ethan, Dylan and Bryson. The family resides in Petersburg. The ceremony concluded with the reading of Creech's retirement orders, formally recognizing his separation from the Army National Guard and placement on the retired list effective Sept. 30. Creech's retirement marks the conclusion of a career spanning enlisted and commissioned service, combat deployment, command assignments and senior leadership positions at the state and national levels. After 40 years in uniform, Creech leaves the Illinois National Guard having served across multiple generations of Soldiers and through some of the organization's most significant missions at home and abroad.

items.title: Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: In a “State of the Force” address Sept. 30, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide push to field autonomous systems, one of several initiatives meant to further his sweeping transformation of the Pentagon. The post Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, Va.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide drive to field autonomous systems, as the Pentagon’s pursues a bullish approach towards artificial intelligence and drone warfare, and unveiled five other initiatives during what he promised will become an annual “State of the Force” address here Sept. 30.

Hegseth plans to launch the Autonomous Warfare Command within a year as a combatant command endowed with “service-like authorities, built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” Hegseth said. Its portfolio will include drones, artificial intelligence, and command and control systems.

Hegseth also announced the creation of a new program office, led by a two-star officer, to ensure military installations can generate their own power to withstand attacks on public grids. Bases in the homeland are increasingly seen as possibly contested enviroments in which the U.S. military must be able to operate while under threat, in a age of increasingly sophisticated cyber attacks and so-called hybrid warfare activities by America’s adversaries.

And he confirmed plans to slash the total number of generals and admirals across the military by 20 percent, a move Air & Space Forces Magazine and other outlets had reported would be part of Hegseth’s speech.

- A new group, dubbed “Project Meridian,” to study the future of warfare led by tech leaders Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, who were in attendance.

- An initiative, called the “Next Great American Base,” to build a new military installation to host 15,000-25,000 service members. Hegseth said governors and adjutant generals from every state will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch locations.

- The creation of five new corps of cadets at Hillsdale College, Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Mississippi State University, and Tuskegee University, which will all be given priority in officer commissioning.

- A new “Office of Religious Affairs” reporting directly to the Secretary of Defense to give chaplains better access to senior leadership.

Exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of senior officers and enlisted from commands across the globe to Quantico for an address outlining his vision for the U.S. military, he spoke this time to an audience of around 500 E-6 enlisted members and O-3 officers, who the Pentagon said were selected by their units for their performance and leadership potential.

Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force Gen. Dan Caine briefly addressed the crowd and introduced Hegseth.

The new Autonomous Warfare Command will drive the design, development, and fielding of autonomous and semi-autonomous capabilities and systems.

“The autonomous and robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades,” Hegseth said. “Civilian leaders can provide direction and urgency, but lasting change must be anchored in military command structures and operationalized by leaders across our joint force.”

The Pentagon is already leaning heavily into autonomy, and the new command is designed to significantly accelerate that effort. Lawmakers in the Senate had proposed the creation of such a combatant command during deliberations for the 2027 defense policy bill. The measure cleared the committee, but the bill is still pending. To be authorized, the House would also have to approve the measure.

It is not yet clear how the new four-star command will be structured, who will lead it, or how it will work with the autonomy efforts already underway within the different services. In a memo, Hegseth wrote the Pentagon plans to work with Congress to stand-up the command by October 1, 2027, a year on from the announcement.

Hegseth said it will start with an interim step, dubbed “Project Agincourt,” named for the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Project Agincourt will draw from existing efforts like the Defense Innovation Unit and the Drone Dominance program, Hegseth said, and pair “operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units.”

Project Agincourt will be guided by DIU director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser, the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School. Creating Autonomous Warfare Command will take place “over the course of several months,” Hegseth said.

The Air Force and Navy are already developing Collaborative Combat Aircraft: semi-autonomous drones designed to work alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force is also pursuing a lower-cost intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drone with autonomous capabilities under its Massed Modular Aircraft program, and the Navy is working to field an unmanned tanker drone, the MQ-25.

The growth of autonomomy and the Penatagon’s future plans to harvest technology with its new command represent the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” Hegseth said.

“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he added, using an acronym for so-called super intelligence, Trump’s favored term for AI.

At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference earlier this month, Air Force leadership made it clear they see autonomous systems as central to the service’s future. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference that while true autonomous aircraft are a “few years off,” the service is leaning heavily into autonomy in its current future Force Design model.

“The FQ-42 and the FQ-44 [Collaborative Combat Aircraft] are autonomous fighters, and then we’re going to have perhaps other platforms that are autonomous, where you don’t actually need a crew to do a fighter mission,” Wilsbach said during a session with reporters. “You just send the aircraft off, and it does its mission because it’s automated.”

The Pentagon has deployed uncrewed surface vessels operationally in the Middle East for a few years for maritime surveillance. This summer, a U.S. Navy drone boat was even able to rescue two downed Army Apache pilots near the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Southern Command, which has been conducting strikes on boats suspected of smuggling drones for over a year, recently established an autonomous warfare branch, that will employ its own uncrewed vessels and aerial intelligence-gathering platforms. On the southern border, the U.S. military is now using 10 uncrewed surface vessels to patrol the Rio Grande River, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs M. Roosevelt Ditlevson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview.

“We’re moving into next-generation tools here that we’re going to employ to make sure that we hold these narcoterrorists at bay,” Ditlevson said, referring to the drug smugglers. “I’m very excited about what is going to happen in the autonomy space and how we’re going to employ these different systems.”

But the Pentagon is automating more than aircraft, ships, and vehicles.

The Pentagon’s Maven Smart System has become a key tool for the U.S. military, a system aggregating sensors, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and command and control as part of the targeting process. Maven is used for operations ranging from targeting assistance in the Middle East to, more recently, counter-drone and anti-smuggling efforts on the southern border.

Ditlevson said AI, through Maven, will also feed into the Pentagon’s sweeping Golden Dome missile defense shield. “Maven Smart System is going to feed into the Golden Dome picture,” he said.

At the border, the Defense Department also uses autonomy software called Fortress, an adaptation of Anduril’s Lattice, which integrates data and sensors using AI. “All of our systems must be compatible with Maven Smart System,” Ditlevson said. “Everything that we have, that data needs to be integrated into Maven and into Lattice.”

To support all these new autonomous systems, Hegseth said, each military service will phase in new military occupational specialties for autonomy.

“We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters,” he said.

Hegseth also said the Pentagon is creating a new initiative called “Fortress America” to ensure military installations are able to generate their own power. The Pentagon has been working on building nuclear microreactors at key U.S. bases in the homeland and has previously said it plans to field a nuclear reactor at a military base by September 2028.

The Air Force in particular is working on a microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, with plans to build more at other bases in the coming years. The service has also explored using alternate power sources like solar panels, geothermal plants, and more to create so-called “microgirds” for bases so they’re not entirely reliant on local civilian power grids.

The drive to give bases their own energy sources is driven by concerns that adversaries may target critical public infrastructure, around 80 percent of which is currently in the commercial sector, to kneecap the military’s ability to generate forces. The Pentagon chief referred to the program as “nation’s insurance policy” in a memo directing the establishment of Fortress America.

“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit, our aircraft keep flying, our command centers never go dark,” Hegseth said.

Hegseth is also slashing the number of general and flag officers, cutting billets by 20 percent. That doubles down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.

“The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said. “And I know because I directed it that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent. So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.”

Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.

The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.

The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and has plans to continue to grow that number.

Hegseth’s address a year about to senior leaders drew a stotic reaction from most generals during politically charged speeches from Hegseth and Trump, keeping with the military apolitical tradition. The troops gave Hegseth a more vocal reception during the address, which lasted around an hour, particularly during his reference to Musk, Luckey, and Gingrich, and Hegseth exited to applause from the troops, though service members appeared to avoid visual reactions to Hegseth’s more idelogical comments. Attendees were separated by branch, and were given a “War Department Field Manual,” a collection speeches by Hegseth with a forward written by Trump. Earlier in the day, the service members in attendance participated in a physical training session with Hegseth on the grounds of the Pentagon.
