org/pubs/research_reports/RRA4254-2. html) Prepared for: Military & Defense Leadership Sponsoring Agency: Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering (USW/R&E) Research Organization: RAND National Defense Research Institute (NDRI) Nature of the Contest: The U.

-China rivalry is not a classic power transition where China inevitably bypasses and replaces the U.

; rather, it is a shift toward a crowded, multipolar hierarchy where unipolar primacy no longer exists.

At its core, it is a long-term struggle between two socio-economic and political systems to determine which can best deliver results and national dynamism for its people.

The Seven-Domain Framework: RAND categorizes national power across seven primary issue areas: Foundational Domains (Highest Priority): Science & Technology and Domestic Economics form the primary drivers of long-term power.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) serves as a critical single fulcrum capable of amplifying capabilities across all other fields.

Supporting Domains: Military, international economics, diplomacy, resources and materials, and information/ideology/culture.

Crosscutting Themes: System and network dynamics alongside society and governance integrate these domains and determine asymmetric advantage.

Competitor Strengths & Vulnerabilities: China: Operates through six overlapping identities (classic great power, developmental state, science/technology hegemon, Leninist dictatorship, civilizational power, and revisionist order-builder).

China commands ~30% of global manufacturing and leads in 66 of 74 critical technologies, but faces deepening vulnerabilities: slowing GDP growth, real estate deflation, local debt, rapid demographic contraction, and structural overreach that alienates neighboring states.

United States: Retains high-end innovation leads in frontier AI and biopharmaceuticals, but faces strategic inflection points driven by mounting public debt, industrial atrophy in critical manufacturing sectors (shipbuilding, batteries, solar), and governance friction.

Strategic Priorities: Success does not require regime change or total displacement.

strategy must focus on domestic renewal in science, technology, and manufacturing; contesting Chinese control over critical digital and supply chain chokepoints; and pairing firm military deterrence with risk-reduction mechanisms to maintain strategic stability.

items.title: People, partnerships, and readiness: Leveraging our lines of effort amid intense wildfire season
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: The Oregon Sentinel Newsletter, Fall 2026 issue.
items.body:
By Brig. Gen. Alan R. Gronewold, Adjutant General, Oregon National Guard

As fall begins and smoke clears across Oregon, our Airmen completed their Grasshopper Fire assignment on August 20. Last week, our Army aircrews flew their final water-bucket missions, and our search and rescue team demobilized as well, marking the end of one of the most challenging wildfire seasons in recent memory. Before discussing the months ahead, I want to reflect on what this summer revealed about our organization.

Since July 20, our aircrews have responded with dedication. What began as a single Black Hawk on MEDEVAC standby expanded into a statewide operation from Army Aviation Support Facility No. 2 in Pendleton, including an HH-60M on search and rescue standby, two HH-60M Black Hawks, and two CH-47 Chinooks conducting water bucket missions on the Hagen Fire in Umatilla County. By the end of operations on the Hagen Fire, our aircrews had completed 1,405 water bucket drops and delivered more than 1.5 million gallons of water, often in challenging, smoke-filled canyons.

In August, 44 Airmen from the 142nd Wing and 173rd Fighter Wing formed two hand crews and deployed to the Mount Hood National Forest for the Grasshopper Fire. This marked the first time our Air Guard hand crews were activated before our Army hand crews. These teams began by wrapping homes, bridges, and signage in fire-resistant material, then shifted to cutting and mopping up containment lines with hand tools alongside experienced wildland crews. As these operations continued, members of the 173rd were activated under Immediate Response Authority to support local authorities with evacuation and wildfire prevention efforts in response to the Wrights Spring Fire.

Also in August, while traveling back to Camp Rilea from another assignment, our Oregon Military Department wildland firefighters responded directly to the Wolf Creek Fire under a mutual aid agreement to assist the incident commander, guiding air and ground support to contain the blaze.

This is true readiness—not just discussed in briefings but demonstrated when we are called on for support, Oregonians. It reflects strong partnerships, working closely with ODF, Cal Fire liaisons, and other agency crews, relying on mutual trust between all elements of our organization to protect lives and property.

And it is People and Culture, too. I stood with our Airmen in Salem as they went through JRSOI just before they boarded buses bound for a fire camp near Warm Springs, watching young men and women who had trained for one mission step forward without hesitation for another. Ten days later, I flew to their fire camp near Tygh Valley aboard one of our own Black Hawks, alongside Brig. Gen. Jenifer Pardy, Command Chief Warrant Officer 5 Lenora Landwehr, Chaplain (Col.) Jacob Scott, and Chief Master Sgt. Brent Cavanias, to thank those same Airmen in person for what they were doing out there. Seeing Guardsmen do exactly what we train for, protecting Oregonians and their property, is what this organization is built for. That willingness to adapt, to go where the state needs them without waiting to be told exactly how, is disciplined initiative in its purest form. It is exactly what I asked of our leaders at the Joint Senior Leader Workshop this past winter, and our formations delivered it this summer under real pressure.

I am proud of every Citizen-Soldier, Airman, and Civilian who spent this summer keeping up with assigned responsibilities while maintaining their training and preparedness to be ready when needed. This last month, we broke ground for a new multi-purpose machine gun range, which has taken more than 20 years to come to fruition. The ceremony in Boardman reflected our commitment to our community partners and to training our Oregon Guard members well into the future. This is just one more example of how each generation, working within the community, continues to ensure our future success. This is what it means to be Oregon’s Service of Choice: an organization Oregonians and people of the United States can rely on, regardless of the mission.

For now, our personnel have returned home to their families and regular units, but the work continues. Annual Training transitions into drill weekends, deployment preparations proceed for overseas missions, and our air crews and hand crews remain ready to respond if needed. I ask every leader to bring the same intensity to garrison operations that our teams demonstrated on the fire line. Know your task, uphold your standards, and take care of your people.

Thank you for everything you have given this state this year. Be Connected. Be Competent. Be Committed.

Always Ready, Always There!

items.title: International Cyber Officers Translate Strategy to Action at DSCU Practical Cyber Implementation Course
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: WASHINGTON — The Defense Security Cooperation University (DSCU) concluded its Practical Cyber Implementation Course Aug. 7, marking the end of two weeks of intensive training for 31 international defense and security professionals from 25 allied and partner countries. The course focused on threat intelligence, secure system design, incident response, artificial intelligence (AI) implementation, and the operational application of cyber policy.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — The Defense Security Cooperation University (DSCU) concluded its Practical Cyber Implementation Course Aug. 7, marking the end of two weeks of intensive training for 31 international defense and security professionals from 25 ally and partner countries. The course focused on threat intelligence, secure system design, incident response, artificial intelligence (AI) implementation, and the operational application of cyber policy.

Designed to help allies and partners bridge the gap between high-level cyber strategy and operational execution, the curriculum underscored the indispensable role cyber defense plays in protecting shared critical infrastructure. It also equipped participants with the skills needed to translate national strategies into tangible, sustainable defense capabilities.

Recent global events have demonstrated that cybersecurity is an essential component of collective security. Participants examined real-world cyber exploitation incidents and assessed their implications for defense planning and response across interconnected environments. Through lectures, case studies, and hands-on exercises, the cohort learned to account for cyber dependencies throughout the strategic planning process.

The course also explored the opportunities and challenges of integrating AI into broader national security frameworks, focusing on the responsible implementation of AI-enabled tools for threat detection, data governance, system security, human oversight, and the mitigation of risks posed by adversarial use of AI.

In addition, participants studied hybrid warfare threats – such as coordinated cyber operations, disinformation, influence activities, and electronic warfare – to develop integrated defense and deterrence strategies that protect public confidence and build systemic resilience.

This practical approach directly translates to active, real-world missions.

“The hands-on exercises were especially helpful in supporting our work to develop policy … and understanding that these frameworks are not just documents, they are, as our instructor said, a ‘living capability that delivers real security,’” remarked one participant.

Beyond technical training, the course serves as a key tool for building institutional human capital and individual capacity. DSCU’s international training, education and advisory services and programs, including cyber, enhance the readiness of partner defense institutions, enabling them to effectively procure, absorb, employ, and sustain capability investments.

To foster mutual understanding, the Field Studies component brought the cohort together to experience the history of the National Capital Region. The group took part in guided tours of historic sites, including the Lincoln Memorial, the White House, the World War II Memorial, the Washington Monument, and the U.S. Capitol Building.

By empowering allies and partners to detect and deter advanced threats and secure their digital infrastructure, this DSCU-led training strengthens the U.S. strategic advantage and burden sharing in a contested digital battlespace.

items.title: Connecticut Military Suicide Awareness and Remembrance Day
items.author: Timothy Koster
items.summary: On May 19, 2026, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont signed Public Act 26-19 into law, which established Military Suicide Awareness and Remembrance Day to be observed annually on Sept. 30th.
items.body: On May 19, 2026, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont signed Public Act 26-19 into law, which established Military Suicide Awareness and Remembrance Day to be observed annually on Sept. 30th. The day is dedicated to honoring veterans and military members lost to suicide, raising awareness of mental health challenges among veterans and military members, and raising awareness of available resources and support systems. “We are here today to remember those that we’ve lost, raise awareness, and make sure that every veteran knows that they are not alone,” said State Rep. Rebecca Martinez, who helped champion the creation of this day. “[In 2025] Governor Lamont issued a proclamation recognizing September 30th, but a proclamation lasts just for a day, we wanted a commitment that would last year-after-year, so we wrote that commitment into law.” State leaders, to include Gov. Lamont, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs Commissioner Ron Welch, Maj. Gen. Francis J. Evon Jr., the adjutant general for the Connecticut National Guard, as well as other lawmakers, observed the day of awareness by holding a press conference at the Legislative Office Building in Hartford, Sept. 30, 2026. “When I took over this chairmanship, I was very nervous about days and symbols because when you pass legislation that is in-and-of-itself a day or a symbol without a concurrent plan to make change, there leaves a lot of room for improvement,” said State Rep. Jaime Foster, House chair of the veterans and military affairs committee. “But what I’ve learned … is that sometimes those symbols carry weight on their own; sometimes those symbols give a sense of community together in a public that wouldn’t always exist otherwise. But when it comes to an issue like this, getting folks help where they need it means that those symbols need to be in their communities when they need it and that the people who might lend a hand to help have the tools and resources to help.” The effort to officially establish Military Suicide Awareness and Remembrance Day was inspired by friends and family of U.S. Army Command Sergeant Maj. Gary F. Sirois, a Plainville, Connecticut resident, who lost his life to suicide on March 1, 2023, at the age of 54. Sirois served more than 20 years in the United States Army and Army Reserve and was a veteran of Operation Iraqi Freedom. “One of the things I’ve learned as a Soldier, and what I know my colleagues here behind me understand, is that the weight of service doesn’t come off when your uniform does,” said State Rep. Hubert Delaney, vice-chairman of the veterans and military affairs committee and a member of the Army Reserve. “It follows your home and it shows up in everything—your health, your family, your finances, your sense of identity, they’re all effected.” “And when it comes to accomplishing the mission, Soldiers were taught from the beginning to look out for the person to our left and to look out for the person to our right,” added Delaney. “We’re told that asking for help when you need it is part of accomplishing that mission and that taking care of people is a part of effective combat lethality. But what my colleagues and I … understand and believe is that that mentality doesn’t just apply to mission readiness, it applies to the health and welfare of our veterans and their families.” On Military Suicide Awareness and Remembrance Day, communities, businesses, and citizens around the state are being encouraged to display a single green light on the evening of September 30, to show veterans who may be struggling with their mental health that they’re not alone and that the people around them support them. “What we hope that what comes next is if you find that resources are inadequate or lacking, that you know you have a room full of leaders who want to make those resources better equipped, better staffed, better resourced, so that we don’t stand here adding another name to this list … and then some day we can make sure that every veteran who needs help gets it when they need it,” said Foster. If you’re a veteran who’s struggling with suicidal thoughts, call the 27/7 veterans crisis line by dialing 988 then pressing 1. You can also text them at 838255. You are not alone.

items.title: Supporting the Community Anytime, Anywhere
items.author: A1C Gabriel Conley
items.summary: In the quiet hours of the night on Sept. 5, 2026, a 37-year-old man’s life was hanging in the balance from chest pain and a potential cardiac arrest slightly east of Sullivan Lake. With local agencies not available to respond to the emergency, they leaned on Team Fairchild and its search and rescue team for aid.
items.body: FAIRCHILD AIR FORCE BASE, Wash.--In the quiet hours of the night on Sept. 5, 2026, a 37-year-old man’s life was hanging in the balance from chest pain and a potential cardiac arrest slightly east of Sullivan Lake. With local agencies not available to respond to the emergency, they leaned on Team Fairchild and its search and rescue team for aid. The patient was located deep in the woods near the Canadian border, which fell under the 36th Rescue Squadron’s response area. When every minute mattered, the call went to Fairchild’s rescue Airmen, who are trained and ready to answer no matter the hour, weather or distance. At 12:23 a.m., the squadron received the alert. Available crew members were notified, and within 30 minutes, a crew for RESCUE 99 had assembled. The crew was composed of Capt. Amber Korpela, aircraft commander; Lt. Col. William Wilkes, copilot; Staff Sgt. Andrew Boothe, special missions’ aviator; and Staff Sgt. Jaime Vergara, medic. Each member of the crew carried a different responsibility, but all shared the same commitment to be ready when someone’s life depended on them. That preparedness is built through the daily training conducted within the squadron. “So, whether that means you have to be prepared physically, mentally, spiritually, you will not be what causes the mission to fail,” said Boothe. As the crew prepared, they faced more than the challenge of the late hour. A fog threatened their mission by limiting visibility along the route. With the crew recognizing these factors, they knew every decision they make, from the aircraft configuration to the route selection, could make or break the mission of transporting the patient to medical care. Before proceeding to the patient, the 36th RQS identified Vergara as a medic, but he was not able to make it to base to take off with the rest of the crew. So, the decision was made to retrieve him after takeoff to complete their crew. With the use of their training and quick coordination amongst each other, the crew planned to pick him up while in the air with a 190-foot hoist extraction. Once the decision was made, they configured the aircraft with the required primary and backup equipment and launched. After retrieving Vergara, the team for RESCUE 99 was fully assembled and ready to proceed toward the patient’s location. “The four of us had flown little, if at all, together before,” Korpela said. “But by falling back on our squadron standards and what we train to do on a daily basis, we were able to come together as a crew very well.” As they approached the search area, the crew faced another critical decision. They had two sets of coordinates for the potential location of the patient. With time working against them, the crew decided to advance with their first set of coordinates and planned to continue to the alternate location if they could not establish visual contact with the patient after multiple orbits. Once they arrived at the first location, the crew began their search for the patient. They relied on communication between each other to search every square foot of the first area, and after a few minutes of searching, they saw a light signal that led them to the correct location. With the patient located, the crew quickly discussed wind conditions, aircraft power requirements, hazards and the hoist-extraction plan. They identified Ione Municipal Airport as the patient transfer location where a Pend Oreille medical team would be awaiting their arrival and began preparing for the recovery. Korpela said the crew’s teamwork, communication and ability to overcome small challenges allowed them to work seamlessly throughout the rescue. The crew initiated the recovery by lowering Vergara nearly 190 feet through the darkness to the patient below. After assessing the patient’s condition, Vergara coordinated with the crew as they hoisted him into the aircraft. The crew then brought Vergara back into the aircraft and prepared to continue the mission. As they approached the transfer location, a fog bank had settled over the area, creating another challenge during the final stage of the mission. An airport beacon near the edge of the fog gave the crew a visual reference as they carefully navigated toward the runway. The crew made a shallow approach beneath the fog bank toward the end of the runway. At 5:35 a.m., they transferred the patient to the medical team standing by and departed to base. For Boothe, the successful transfer represented the commitment that drives every rescue mission, regardless of the conditions or challenges they face. “We will always do our best and do everything in our ability to get you to safety in as timely a manner as possible and make sure we get you out of the situation,” Boothe said. By the time the crew returned to Fairchild AFB, the crew had overcome fatigue, limited visibility, changing weather conditions and a complex hoist extraction to transport the patient to safety. The mission became the 36th Rescue Squadron’s 718th save and was a reminder that, when a call for help comes in, the squadron’s Airmen are prepared to answer.

items.title: Making my mark | Sgt. Stlouis' journey through training
items.author: LCpl Donovan Pimentel
items.summary: U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Khaleel Stlouis, from Florida, a reconfigurable transportable consolidated automated support system technician with Marine Aviation Logistics Squadron (MALS) 14, Marine Aircraft Group 14, 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing, speaks on his journey through collecting Marine Corps qualifications and how he uses it to lead Marines at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina, S
items.body: U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Khaleel Stlouis, from Florida, a reconfigurable transportable consolidated automated support system technician with Marine Aviation Logistics Squadron (MALS) 14, Marine Aircraft Group 14, 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing, speaks on his journey through collecting Marine Corps qualifications and how he uses it to lead Marines at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina, Sep. 29, 2026. Donovan Pimentel)

items.title: ONR’s I2D, TECHx Events Connect Industry Innovators with Naval S&T Priorities
items.author: Cherish Gilmore
items.summary: The Office of Naval Research (ONR) concluded a week of direct engagement with industry on Sept. 24. It hosted Innovation Industry Days (I2D) Sept. 21-22, followed by Focus Area Technical Exchanges, known as ONR TECHx, Sept. 23-24, all held at George Mason University’s Mason Square in Ballston.
items.body:
The Office of Naval Research (ONR) concluded a week of direct engagement with industry on Sept. 24. It hosted Innovation Industry Days (I2D) Sept. 21-22, followed by Focus Area Technical Exchanges, known as ONR TECHx, Sept. 23-24, all held at George Mason University’s Mason Square in Ballston.

The back-to-back events brought together approximately 300 participants from the defense, commercial and emerging technology sectors to accelerate warfighter capabilities for the Navy and Marine Corps.

"What we saw this week was industry showing up ready to solve real problems, not hypothetical ones,” said Dr. Thomas Fu, ONR Executive Director performing the duties of Chief of Naval Research. “The direct dialogue between our program officers and our partners is exactly how we close technology gaps faster and get capability into the hands of Sailors and Marines sooner."

During I2D, ONR leaders and technical experts shared 15-year science and technology roadmaps spanning 11 Focus Areas, highlighting the research opportunities, challenges and technology needs facing the Fleet and Force. Focus Areas included Artificial Intelligence and Autonomy; Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Cyber, Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (C5ISR) and Naval Space; Directed Energy and Kinetic Systems; Materials and Electronics; Human and Biological Systems; Manufacturing; Naval Engineering; Naval Aerospace; Ocean Atmosphere and Space; Power and Energy; and Undersea Systems.

The event’s structure — combining large-group portfolio briefings with smaller, focused office hours — was designed to move beyond one-way information sharing and toward substantive, two-way technical exchange.

ONR TECHx built on those broader briefings with focused exchanges and one-on-one discussions between industry partners and ONR program officers and technical leads.

More than 200 of the companies present were new performers for ONR.

Event organizers noted the smaller-group format gave attendees the chance to dive deeper into specific research priorities, share relevant capabilities and explore potential pathways for collaboration.

I2D and ONR TECHx offer more frequent opportunities for technological exchange with the Navy and Marine Corps’ focus areas.

items.title: Department of the Air Force awards F-15EX Lot 7 contract for 22 aircraft
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: The Department of the Air Force awarded Boeing a contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II aircraft under Lot 7 – preserving the buying power of congressionally provided reconciliation funding and sustaining F-15EX production.
items.body: By Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio – The Department of the Air Force awarded Boeing a contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II aircraft under Lot 7 – preserving the buying power of congressionally provided reconciliation funding and sustaining F-15EX production. The Lot 7 agreement accounts for current programmatic realities, including the effects of the 2025 production disruption and broader inflation across the defense industrial base. Through focused, complex negotiations, the F-15 Program Office and Boeing reached an agreement that maintains the procurement of all 22 Lot 7 aircraft within available funding. “Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production,” said Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, Portfolio Acquisition Executive for the Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate. “The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future.” The F-15EX is a modern, multirole heavy fighter that builds on the proven F-15 design. The aircraft incorporates advanced avionics, large-area displays, digital backbone architecture and enhanced survivability capabilities. It is intended to replace aging F-15C and F-15D aircraft while providing a platform for continued modernization as operational requirements evolve. The Lot 7 award also demonstrates the application of the Secretary of War’s acquisition transformation principles by empowering an integrated F-15 negotiation team to rapidly deliver capability. The team synchronized expertise across functional areas, elevated issues requiring senior-level decisions, and maintained accountability for cost, schedule, and aircraft quantity—demonstrating the speed, disciplined execution, and mission-focused accountability central to the Warfighting Acquisition System. This award followed extensive collaboration among program management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management, logistics and other acquisition professionals. The team assessed the impacts of changing production conditions and inflation, aligned the aircraft procurement with available funding, and completed the action before the fiscal-year deadline. Senior Department leaders supported timely coordination and decision-making throughout the process. Their engagement enabled the team to address complex affordability and execution challenges while maintaining focus on the program’s operational purpose: delivering modern fighter capability to Airmen. "The Lot 7 award demonstrates what is possible when the acquisition enterprise moves with purpose, remains accountable to the taxpayer and stays focused on delivering capability to the warfighter,” said Col. Jonathan Varoli, System Program Manager of the directorate's F-15 Program Office. “This effort brought together the right expertise, at the right time, to achieve an outcome that strengthens the F-15EX program and supports the future fighter force.” The Department of the Air Force will continue working with Boeing to support rapid, affordable and sustainable F-15EX production. The Lot 7 award sustains the program’s near-term production effort while the Air Force continues to assess future requirements and acquisition strategies.

items.title: Mental Health and Your Security Clearance: Why Transparent Reporting and Seeking Care Strengthen National Security
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: A reminder about mental health and security clearances.
items.body:
By Lorra Ballou, AFLCMC Personnel Security and Insider Threat Program Manager

WRIGHT-PATTERSON AFB, Ohio (AFLCMC) - Uniform and civilian airmen with security clearances often handle complex missions and may navigate intense stress. For decades, an enduring misconception has lingered that acknowledging a mental health challenge or seeking counseling will immediately jeopardize a clearance or even derail a career.

Security clearance vetting guidelines and data from across government security agencies tell a very different story. Between 2012 and 2023, more than 7.5 million adjudicative actions were taken, with less than 200 denials/revocations solely for psychological conditions.

In each of these adverse actions, it was not the underlying mental health challenge that resulted in denial/revocation, but rather additional factors like not adhering to medical treatment plans, refusal to seek care in the face of acute impairment, or intentional concealment of information.

What Conditions and Situations Must Be Reported?

There are specific psychological conditions that require reporting to security. Security questionnaires (such as the Standard Form 86) and Continuous Vetting guidelines focus strictly on conditions that could impair cognitive faculties, judgment, or emotional stability. Specific reportable events include:

Legal determination of mental incompetence

Court-ordered mental health treatments or evaluations

Inpatient psychiatric hospitalizations

Specific conditions that may directly impair judgment, reliability, or impulse control (such as schizophrenia, antisocial personality disorder, or bipolar mood disorder)

Self-assessed mental health concerns where the individual feels their reliability or judgment is substantially affected

How Mental Health is Evaluated in Personnel Vetting:

Understanding what happens behind the scenes can demystify the vetting process and alleviate anxiety surrounding reporting requirements. After a psychological event is reported to security, here is what happens:

Security Managers capture relevant details such as treatment provider’s information, dates of treatment, or specific diagnoses. This information is provided to Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) Trust Decision Adjudications (TD(A)).

A trained adjudicator with DCSA TD(A) uses a whole-person concept to adjudicate the individual’s security clearance eligibility. The medical practitioner may be contacted for treatment records or professional opinions regarding the individual’s ability to safeguard classified information, and in cases where questions remain regarding operational fitness, an independent psychological evaluation may be requested. Compliance with treatment recommendations and transparency through self-reporting are also considered favorably as part of the whole-person concept.

Depending on the severity of the situation, the Commander/Director may elect to suspend access to classified information locally, until a final adjudicative determination is made by TD(A). This local access suspension is a tool to ensure information and assets are not at risk until the concern is confidently mitigated. A local access suspension does not mean a loss of security clearance eligibility; only DCSA TD(A) can make the final determination for security clearance eligibility.

Help-Seeking is a Professional Strength

Personnel security policies are structured around the reality that mental health challenges often happen and are treatable. Eligibility hinges on whether a condition is managed effectively, not on whether a condition exists.

Seeking care is a proactive step that protects health, strengthens operational resilience, and preserves careers. Transparency and treatment remain the clearest, most reliable paths to maintaining long-term security clearance eligibility.

If you are experiencing challenges with your personal well-being which could impact your clearance eligibility, reach out to your security office early. These experts will help you navigate the clearance eligibility process and will assist you with proper guidance and available resources.

items.title: A Lifetime of Service: Dennis D’Angelo Bids Farewell After 48 Years Shaping Air Force Readiness
items.author: James Varhegyi
items.summary: AFLCMC's executive director retires after a lifetime of military service.
items.body:
WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio (AFLCMC) - During a milestone retirement ceremony on Sept. 28 at the National Museum of the United States Air Force, Dennis D’Angelo, executive director, Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC), officially concluded a distinguished 48-year federal career.

Surrounded by senior military leaders, elected officials, family, and colleagues, D’Angelo was honored for a lifetime of service that directly transformed how the United States Air Force acquires, maintains, and sustains its global fleet.

His extraordinary journey - comprising 30 years in uniform as an Air Force officer and 18 years as a civilian leader - spans two-thirds of the independent Air Force’s 79-year history.

From Air Mobility Pilot to Senior Executive

D’Angelo began his Air Force journey as an Air Mobility pilot, rising through the ranks to retire as a colonel in 2008 after 30 years of active-duty service.

Far from stepping away, he transitioned seamlessly into federal civilian service, putting on a business suit to continue supporting the warfighter.

His early civilian assignments included crucial logistical oversight for U.S. Africa Command and U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) in Tampa, Florida, from 2014 to 2017.

During intense operational demands, D’Angelo managed a $1 billion theater recapitalization of airfields and ports and oversaw $1.1 billion in organize, train, and equip (OT&E) programs for partner nations across the Middle East.

In 2017, D’Angelo entered the Senior Executive Service (SES) as the civilian leader of the 448th Supply Chain Management Wing at Tinker Air Force Base, Oklahoma. There, he slashed contracting flow times by 76% and introduced an innovative parts procurement model that saved $90 million across the five-year defense budget.

By 2020, as the Air Force Sustainment Center’s executive director, he championed robotics and additive manufacturing, leading to the certification of 94 advanced manufacturing products and expanding the organic industrial base.

Modernizing an Enterprise of 21,000

For the past three years, D’Angelo served as AFLCMC’s senior-most civilian, guiding a massive enterprise of over 21,000 military, civilian, and contractor personnel operating across 84 geographic locations.

As part of the AFLCMC leadership team, he helped spearhead a fundamental paradigm shift - moving the Air Force away from an isolated, platform-by-platform acquisition approach - toward a fully integrated architecture that synchronizes acquisition, logistics, and sustainment enterprise-wide.

Retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Mark Ramsay led the ceremony and also presided over D’Angelo’s retirement from active duty. Ramsay commented that D’Angelo understood the fundamental value of people.

“It is all about people,” explained Ramsay. “It’s all about professional and personal relationships and development of people, and Denny does that better than anyone in the room”

During his tenure at AFLCMC, D’Angelo led efforts that yielded an enterprise-wide 7% boost in fleet readiness, cut F-35 airworthiness review times nearly in half through collaboration with the Navy and NASA, and achieved $4.6 billion in overall cost avoidance.

He also drove a revolutionary engine repair concept that cut replacement costs by 95%. That change saved $800 million alone andachieved full remediation of the Air Force’s military equipment valuation weakness across $94 billion in aircraft assets.

During the ceremony, D’Angelo was presented with both the Department of the Air Force Decoration for Exceptional Civilian Service and the Outstanding Civilian Career Service Award.

Partnership, Leadership, and the Road Ahead

Throughout the event, it was underscored that D’Angelo’s accomplishments were deeply shared with his wife of 35 years, Sandy.

“Sandy is the reason why Denny was able to succeed at everything he did,” said Ramsay. “They’re a wonderful family, and I know Sandy will do anything to help the Air Force as an institution and do anything to help Denny succeed in both his personal and his professional life. The fact that he has done so well, for so long, is as much a testament to Sandy as it is to Denny.”

Sandy played a central and influential role throughout D’Angelo’s career, serving as his primary support system and partner across his military and civilian service.

During the ceremony, Sandy came forward to present Dennis with his Air Force civilian retirement pin.

She also received the United States Air Force Spouse Appreciation Certificate, signed by the Secretary of the Air Force, which formally recognized her contributions, sacrifices, and support that provided strength and purpose throughout his career.

During his remarks, D’Angelo paid warm tribute to the Air Force’s Chief Master Sergeants (E-9s), echoing a guiding principle from his 48 years: "If you want to get something done, you give it to a chief."

He also echoed Ramsay’s words about his people-focused approach to his work.

“If you take care of your people, they’re going to take care of the mission tomorrow,” said D’Angelo. “It was always about the people who made the mission possible.”

He related that to how he sees the importance of the work done at AFLCMC.

“The real customer is the young airman or soldier in harm's way somewhere in the world waiting for the weapon system to show up,” said D’Angelo. “They will not know our names, nor should they. They just want to return home to their loved ones. Don’t let us be the reason they don’t”

D’Angelo concluded his remarks with a favorite quote he shares at every opportunity he gets.

“Never underestimate our impact on the mission by our proximity to the fight." He added, “What you do six, seven, eight, ten thousand miles away... enables the fight.”

items.title: Gray Flag: making sure systems connect the first time
items.author: Michael Smith
items.summary: Military aircraft flew more than 750 sorties at Gray Flag 2026, which ended Sept. 25, to expose integration problems before fleet aviators meet them on deployment.
items.body: Military aircraft flew more than 750 sorties at Gray Flag 2026, which ended Sept. 25, to expose integration problems before fleet aviators meet them on deployment. Gray Flag, held annually at Naval Base Ventura County Point Mugu, is the naval aviation test community's premier large-force test event. This year's was the largest to date, topping the roughly 600 sorties flown in 2024 and more than 500 in 2025. The two-week event drew more than 3,000 participants from more than 150 organizations, and crews logged more than 2,000 flight hours covering hundreds of multi-domain test objectives for the fleet and joint force. On a single day alone, 78 aircraft launched for one test event, a Gray Flag record. Point Mugu pumped more than 1.3 million gallons of jet fuel during the event. The Royal Australian Air Force, Royal Canadian Air Force and Royal Air Force joined U.S. Navy and Air Force test teams, along with surface and subsurface participants. Together they checked whether aircraft, weapons, communication systems and networks can pass data and work together. Royal Australian Air Force Wing Commander Trent Baldry, commanding officer of No. 1 Squadron, said Gray Flag gives Australia insight into its interoperability with partners that it could not gain on its own. "We leave much more informed with respect to future capabilities that enable Australia to shape our requirements for future projects and future platform upgrades that increase our lethality and survivability," Baldry said. Naval Test Wing Pacific and Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 9 hosted the event. They led test execution with Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division, which manages the Gray Flag program and operates the Point Mugu Sea Range, a 36,000-square-mile instrumented range. "Our range, combined with other test and training ranges around us, gives us the space and instrumentation to test new systems the way the joint force will use them," said Rear Adm. Keith Hash, NAWCWD commander. "We want to find the problems here, fix them here and make sure what we send to the fleet works when the warfighter needs it." Simulations model the links between platforms working as designed, so they can miss problems that only surface when data has to cross between aircraft in flight, said Capt. Christopher Putre, commodore of Naval Test Wing Pacific. "You need all your lightning bolts from the various domains to reach each other in order to achieve success in a joint fight," Putre said. "And until we test that in scenarios like this, we just don't know it's going to work." Those links get hardest to hold when crews arrive somewhere new, especially on deployment, said Marine Lt. Col. Timothy "Little Buddy" Burchett, commanding officer of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 31. Testing alongside partner nations lets teams find and correct those issues or work around them so fleet aviators can be "lethal from day one," Burchett said. Burchett has flown in Gray Flag as a pilot. His squadron, based at China Lake, is one of the event's founding squadrons. "If we have done our jobs correctly at Gray Flag ... aviators will start systems and be able to have solid interoperability with the Joint Force on the first try," Burchett said. "Ideally, fleet aviators will directly see the fruits of Gray Flag every day; they just won't realize it." Adam Madson, Gray Flag program manager at NAWCWD, dealt with the same challenge as an EA-18G Growler pilot. At Clark Air Base in the Philippines, he said, he had to work out how to network with Air Force units and talk to a ship. Madson said a flaw found after delivery means new training and a workaround for aircrew. Gray Flag, he said, is the last point where testers can answer open questions about a system and still change it before it reaches the fleet. "If we don't answer them here, our warfighter's going to answer them in combat," Madson said. "It will not be as lethal and it'll be much more difficult to survive." Putre said a test that falls short still counts as a success when the team knows why and can point engineers to the fix. Analysts will use the event's petabytes of test data to inform the tactics aviators fly and the specifications engineers test against, Madson said.

items.title: US Air Force awards $2.38B contract to Boeing for 22 F-15EX
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: The service awarded Boeing a contract for 22 more F-15EX aircraft, bringing the number to a total of 120 to be manufactured by the defense company.
items.body:
The U.S. Air Force tapped Boeing for a $2.38 billion contract to produce 22 F-15EX Eagle II aircraft, using previously available funds from the congressionally provided reconciliation to maintain procurement before the fiscal year deadline.

The award is under Lot 7, which accounts for current programmatic realities, according to a recent release, meaning it includes the effects of the 2025 production disruptions and inflation in the defense industrial base.

“Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production,” Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, portfolio acquisition executive for the Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate, said in the release.

“The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future,” he continued.

The agreement showcases the usage of the Pentagon’s acquisition transformation principles by allowing for the integration of an F-15 negotiation team to boost delivery, the release highlights.

The funding for the Lot 7 agreement came from the 2026 budget and a subsequent reconciliation package, titled One Big Beautiful Bill, that required the funds to be spent before the fiscal year ends Sept. 30 or face cuts to the amount allotted.

The service did not include the agreement’s cost, but Boeing announced the $2.38 billion price tag in a separate company release. Boeing is now under contract with the Air Force for Lots 1 through 7, bringing the total number of aircraft to be manufactured to 120.

The F-15EX is built on the F-15 design and is meant to replace the aging F-15C and F-15D aircraft. Described as a multirole heavy fighter, the aircraft includes advanced avionics, large-area displays, digital backbone architecture and increased survivability capabilities.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: Navy Medicine personnel train patient transport capabilities at Naval Medical Center Camp Lejeune
items.author: PO2 Justin Woods
items.summary: Expeditionary Medical Facility Kilo (EMF-Kilo) focused on patient transport during a training evolution for Navy Medicine personnel stationed across Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune. The training, held Sept. 23-24 at the NMCCL Healthcare Simulation and Bio skills Center, focused on specific competencies and operational experiences. Teams ran through scenarios of on-site emergency care, transport to a simulated field hospital, continued medical care, and then movement to an established medical faci
items.body: CAMP LEJEUNE, NC – Expeditionary Medical Facility Kilo (EMF-Kilo) focused on patient transport during a training evolution for Navy Medicine personnel stationed across Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune. The training, held Sept. 23-24 at the NMCCL Healthcare Simulation and Bio skills Center, focused on specific competencies and operational experiences. Teams ran through scenarios of on-site emergency care, transport to a simulated field hospital, continued medical care, and then movement to an established medical facility. “This unit-level training was for skill sustainment practice,” said Lieutenant Louis Martinez, EMF-Kilo assistant training officer. “It allowed us to practice managing patients in the field, working as a team, patient movement, and most importantly documentation.” EMF-Kilo worked with 2nd Medical Battalion to simulate field casualties that would typically be encountered in austere environments and simulate the transport of patients before, during, and after emergency medical treatment. “Day one was mostly point-of-injury site treatment and transportation between 2nd Medical Battalion and ourselves,” said Martinez. “Day two consisted of prolonged field care for overnight patients prior to patient movement.” The hospital corpsmen and medical officers were able to completeprocedures they may not always be able to perform on a regular basis to preserve lifesaving medical skills. “This training was helpful because I was able to do things like inserting chest tubes and improving upon sterile processing techniques, all in a stressful environment, and ensuring I remembered how to do everything properly,” said Hospitalman Haley Kaeding, an EMF Kilo hospital corpsman. The training additionally provided Sailors with the opportunity to perfect communication skills. “One thing this training highlighted is how important communication really is, because you’re moving patients to multiple different locations, and proper turnover is really important when someone’s life is on the line,” said Martinez. Modern medical technology is not readily available in combat zones meaning proper verbal communication and turnover is vital to saving lives. According to Lieutenant Gonzalez, proper paper charting is essential when connectivity with electronic health systems – like Military Health System (MHS) GENESIS – is not an option. This training ensured physicians and corpsmen could properly create and follow a paper trail that could include ordering lab tests, radiology scans, and pharmaceutical medications, and tracking results and delivery. “We cycle new Sailors through this training each quarter to maximize exposure to the operational constraints we may be asked to work through in a deployed setting,” said Commander Claire Vidrine, EMF Kilo interim executive officer. The training ended with a debriefing session where Sailors highlighted challenges and successes with the common goal to ensure they are capable of providing world-class care when called to mobilize anywhere. EMF-Kilo is the expeditionary readiness platform attached to Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command Camp Lejeune and is comprised of approximately hundreds of personnel ready to deploy field hospital capabilities during humanitarian or combat mission.

items.title: NAVFAC Southwest Awards Contract to Construct Warehouses in Bandiana, Australia
items.author: KristaK Cummins
items.summary: SAN DIEGO — Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Southwest awarded a $28,518,010 (USD) task order contract Sept. 28 to Icon SI (AUST) Pty Ltd. of Victoria, Australia for construction of two new warehouses at Albury Wodonga Military Area in North Bandiana, Australia as part of the Fiscal Year 2026 United States Unspecified Minor Military Construction program.
items.body: SAN DIEGO — Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Southwest awarded a $28,518,010 (USD) task order contract Sept. 28 to Icon SI (AUST) Pty Ltd. of Victoria, Australia for construction of two new warehouses at Albury Wodonga Military Area in North Bandiana, Australia as part of the Fiscal Year 2026 United States Unspecified Minor Military Construction program. The task order includes options to outfit the warehouses with furniture, fixtures, and equipment for a total cumulative value of $28,594,510. The projects will construct two new warehouses which include parking, storage, office spaces, restrooms, fire suppression systems, electrical power, and other amenities that will make the buildings suitable for use. “These projects are examples of the ongoing partnership between the U.S. and Australia as critical infrastructure is built to support U.S. and Australian military long term equipment storage for training exercises in Australia and within the Pacific theater,” said NAVFAC Southwest Pacific Deterrence Initiative Program Manager Earl Estrella. Work will be performed in North Bandiana, Australia with an expected completion date in April 2028. This project falls under the U.S. Force Posture Initiative (USFPI), which aims to demonstrate the strength and commitment of the US-Australia alliance, enhance deterrence, and promote regional stability and security. The procurement for this project was swift and utilized an Indo-Pacific multiple award construction contract vehicle to promote competition and success. The project marks another construction milestone for the United States and Australia in implementing the agreement by both governments to establish Northern and Southern nodes within the combined logistics networks in Australia under the Force Posture Agreement, announced at the Australia-U.S. Ministerial Consultations (AUSMIN) 2025. NAVFAC Southwest supports planning, design, construction, real estate, environmental and public works for U.S Navy, Marine Corps, Army, Air Force and other supported federal agencies in the Southwest region and in various locations within the PACOM theater to include Southern Australia.

items.title: NAVFAC Southeast Awards $49.5M Job Order Contract for NS Guantanamo Bay
items.author: Jeffrey Hamlin
items.summary: NAVFAC Southeast has awarded a $49.5 million Job Order Contract to Centerra Integrated Services LLC for facility sustainment and minor construction at Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, through September 2031. This pre-negotiated, indefinite-delivery contracting tool bypasses administrative delays to rapidly deliver vital maintenance for critical infrastructure—including utilities, housing, piers, and airfield operations, ensuring continuous operational readiness at the isolated installation wh
items.body:
Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Southeast announced Sept. 22 the award of a $49.5 million multiyear job order contract to support facility sustainment, restoration and minor construction at Naval Station (NS) Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

Because NS Guantanamo Bay has no local commercial alternatives for utilities, housing or medical support, rapid maintenance delivery is critical to operational readiness.

“At an overseas installation like NS Guantanamo Bay, procurement agility directly supports operational readiness,” said Cory Iselin, a supervisory contract specialist with NAVFAC Southeast. “This job order contract reduces administrative delays, allowing our team to deliver timely engineering solutions and infrastructure improvements when installation commands and warfighters need them most.”

A job order contract, or JOC, is an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contracting tool based on pre-negotiated unit pricing from standardized industry cost databases. Rather than requiring separate solicitations for individual jobs, the JOC enables the government to rapidly issue task orders as infrastructure needs arise.

Centerra Integrated Services LLC, based in Herndon, Virginia, will perform the work across the installation. The contract supports utility networks, airfield operations, deepwater piers, communications facilities, barracks, family housing, clinics and recreational sites.

Work will focus on mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems, as well as roofing, building envelope repairs, interior renovations, and environmental services including lead and asbestos abatement.

Work under the contract is scheduled for completion by September 2031.

About Naval Station Guantanamo Bay

Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, established in 1903, serves as a strategic logistics and operational hub. It is the premier southern-most deep-water naval outpost in the Caribbean, supporting maritime interdiction, humanitarian assistance, and joint force training.

About Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Southeast

Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) Southeast, headquartered in Jacksonville, Florida, provides planning, design, construction, contracting, environmental services, real estate and facility maintenance for the U.S. Navy, Marine Corps, Army, Air Force, Space Force, and other federal agencies across the Southeast. Its area of responsibility covers installations from Charleston, South Carolina, to Corpus Christi, Texas, and extends south to Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

The post Air Force Names 7 to Vie for New MMA Drone Program appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Air Force and the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit have narrowed the field to seven companies which will be invited to compete to develop low-cost, semi-autonomous drones to succeed the MQ-9A Reaper, multiple sources confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero all made the cut to continue to develop their candidates for the Massed Modular Aircraft. The companies got the word Sept. 30.

The Air Force and DIU did not immediately respond to queries. Spokespeople from each of the companies either declined to comment or did not respond to queries. It is unclear how many companies submitted proposals, and therefore how many firms were cut from the competition.

An industry source said each company will now submit a proposal to build a prototype MMA.

The Air Force wants to field 500 MMAs by 2032, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.

DIU—an acquisition office created to tap into commercial and non-traditional suppliers—sought on July 7 proposals for cheap, attritable drones that could take on the MQ-9’s trademark missions of persistent intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and strike. The Air Force soon confirmed it was working with DIU on the concept.

The solicitation followed the loss of dozens of MQ-9s in operations against Iran earlier this year. DIU said at the time that the military’s reliance on “exquisite” aircraft that cost $30 million or more per tail has become “unsustainable against adversaries utilizing layered defenses enabled by increasingly low-cost antiaircraft capabilities.”

The MQ-9As that were lost did not cost that much, but General Atomics no longer makes that model and instead is offering a larger MQ-9B that can approach or exceed the $30 million level, depending on how it is equipped.

MMA is aiming for a lower price point. DIU’s solicitation sought drones that could fly together in groups large enough to overwhelm an enemy, even if several were shot down, while also forcing the enemy to expend precious anti-aircraft munitions. The Air Force must be able to affordably replace aircraft lost without busting the budget.

Air Force leaders said in a Sept. 3 briefing that they expect to pay about $10 million per MMA airframe, plus whatever sensors or other capabilities are added to it. During that briefing, Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said Secretary Meink pushed to accelerate the MMA fielding schedule in the wake of the Iran losses. Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel, DIU’s military deputy, told reporters that the Pentagon wants to see a prototype within a year of issuing a contract, and field it at scale as soon as 2029.

Responding to the summer solicitation, industry rapidly moved to pitch their concepts. General Atomics pitched a new drone called Wildfire that could carry at least two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, four Joint Strike Missiles, or a similar combination of heavy stand-off weapons.

Swarm Aero, a California startup, proposed a new Group 5 drone dubbed Gamera, and displayed a full-scale model at the Air, Space & Cyber conference.

items.title: White House nominates next general to helm US Space Command
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: If confirmed, Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr. would take over command from Gen. Stephen Whiting after his upcoming retirement.
items.body:
The White House on Tuesday nominated Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr. to lead the U.S. Space Command as its general, according to a congressional notice.

Miller is currently the deputy chief of Space Operations, Strategy, Plans, Programs and Requirements. He will, if confirmed, take over Space Command after his predecessor, Gen. Stephen Whiting, steps down from command toward the end of the year or the beginning of the next.

“Congratulations to Lt. Gen. Miller on his nomination to serve as Commander, U.S. Space Command,” Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said in a social media post. “He is an exceptional guardian who has represented our service with distinction, and we believe he is a strong candidate for this critical joint leadership role.”

Prior to his current post, Miller served as the commander of Space Operations Command at Peterson Space Force Base, Colorado. He also served as the special assistant to the vice chief of space operations at Peterson and has held roles commanding guardians and airmen at the squadron, group and wing levels at various bases.

If confirmed, Miller will become the fourth commander of SPACECOM since its reestablishment in 2019, at a time when U.S. leaders are increasingly emphasizing the role of space in operations and the nation’s defense.

The nomination comes on the heels of Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink revealing that the department has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force from “hostile adversary action.” Keeping details sparse, he declined to say what type of weapon it is and reasserted its necessity for deterrence.

Officials have touted space’s role in recent missions, such as Operation Epic Fury, calling its capability essential to the joint force.

“During Operation Epic Fury, our components, notably at U.S. Central Command and Space Command with support from components at European Command and Pacific Command, demonstrated that guardians are not supporting from the sidelines as a ‘nice to have,’ but we are delivering spacepower directly into the fight as a ‘need to have,’” Schiess said during his keynote at the mid-September Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference.

As commander, Miller will be responsible for the space domain while providing space-enabled combat effects across the world, bearing combat command authority over joint warfighters operating ground and space-based systems.

Miller would succeed Whiting, who has held the position since January 2024 after being nominated by former President Joe Biden the year prior and confirmed in December 2024.

Whiting previously served as commander of Space Operations Command and held numerous positions across U.S. Strategic Command, Air Force headquarters and the Office of the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

A formal confirmation hearing for Miller has yet to be set by the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: Unique America: Experiencing the lesser-known traditions that define the Marine Corps’ Oldest Post
items.author: CPT Lauri Schleicher
items.summary: WASHINGTON -- Audiences around the world recognize the precision of Marines marching across the parade deck at Marine Barracks Washington, but much of the training and responsibility behind those performances happens far from public view.
